EEXI is the existing fleet-adapted sibling of EEDI, which is mandatory for new ships: EEDI is calculated once when the ship is designed, while EEXI is applied as a one-time threshold to ships already at sea. As they both measure design (technical) efficiency, they should be considered alongside the CII, which measures the annual operational performance of the ship: EEXI answers the question 'how efficiently the ship is designed', while CII answers the question 'how efficiently the ship is actually operated'. If compliance is not achieved, the IAPP certificate will not be renewed and the ship will not be able to sail internationally.

The basic idea is simple: how much CO₂ does a ship produce for each tonne of cargo it carries, each nautical mile? EEXI'nin temelinde, geminin teorik karbo: The basis of EEXI is a formula that measures the theoretical carbon efficiency of the ship: the denominator is the total CO₂ emissions based on the power of the main and auxiliary engines, their specific fuel consumption and the carbon factor of the fuel; The denominator represents the product of the ship's carrying capacity (DWT or GT) and the reference speed (Vref). The result is the 'achieved EEXI' in gCO₂/tonne·miles and must not exceed the 'required EEXI' reference line determined by ship type and size; this baseline is based on the reduction factors in the EEDI phases. Various correction factors go into the calculation: factors such as capacity correction (fi), cubic capacity correction (fc) and ice class/weather condition. EEXI is a fixed one-time threshold that evaluates the theoretical efficiency of the ship's design, not its actual navigational data.

Ek I, gemilerden petrol deşarjını sıkı k: Annex I imposes strict conditions on oil discharge from ships: engine room bilge can only be pumped through an oil-water separator (OWS) to contain less than 15 ppm oil, while cargo area discharges are controlled by cargo oil residue monitoring device (ODME) and slop tank arrangement. The double-hull requirement became the structural standard for tankers after the Exxon Valdez and similar accidents. Annex II divides bulk hazardous liquids (NLS) into categories X, Y, Z and OS according to their environmental hazard; Tank washing, prewash and residue discharge rules are different for each category. Ek I, MARPOL'ün en eski ve en ayrıntılı: Annex I is MARPOL's oldest and most detailed annex; It prevents oil from mixing into the sea from both the engine room and the cargo area with separate regimes. On the engine room side, bilge water can be pumped only after passing it through the oil-water separator (OWS) and reducing the oil content to below 15 ppm; The 15 ppm alarm and automatic stop ensure this. In the cargo area, ODME (Oil Discharge Monitoring Equipment), which monitors the cargo oil discharge for tankers, slop tank arrangement that collects dirty washing water, and Crude Oil Washing (COW) systems, which reduce the residue by washing the tank with its own cargo in crude oil tankers, are envisaged. Separated ballast tanks (SBT) prevent ballast water from coming into contact with oil. The double hull structure, which became mandatory after the 1990s, reduces the risk of rupture of the cargo tank in collisions and groundings. All these operations are recorded in the Oil Log Book (ORB Part I – machinery, Part II – cargo).

Ek VI, MARPOL'ün en hızlı evrilen bölümü: Annex VI is the most rapidly evolving part of MARPOL and contains several separate regimes. The fuel sulfur limit for sulfur oxides (SOx) is 0.50% globally, 0.10% in Emission Control Areas (ECA/SECA); This is achieved with low sulfur fuel or an exhaust gas cleaning system (scrubber). There are Tier I-II-III limits for nitrogen oxides (NOx), depending on the year of manufacture of the engine and the driving region; Tier III applies only in NECA regions. The department also regulates the control of ozone depleting substances (ODS – halon, CFC), the VOC management plan for crude oil tankers and approved ship incinerators. Most importantly, it is the home of the energy efficiency regime: EEDI for new ships, EEXI for existing ships; CII measures annual operational carbon intensity; SEEMP is the management plan of this performance. Annex VI thus builds a bridge from classical pollution control to greenhouse gas reduction.

The proliferation of electronic navigation systems has required the bridge to manage multiple digital information streams. Cross-checking is based on the principle of verifying each source by comparing location and environmental information obtained from different and independent sources. This principle directly addresses the danger of blind reliance on a single sensor and is essential to meet COLREG's obligation of appropriate stewardship.

Cross-checking is not just a 'good practice'; It is a procedure clearly prescribed in the IMO and STCW guidelines on electronic navigation. SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 19 requires the use of suitable means of navigation and verification of their reliability. The discipline of cross-checking allows the navigator to recognize system errors and GPS/ECDIS anomalies before they become real dangers.

EPIRB (Emergency Position Indicating Rad: EPIRB (Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon) and SART (Search and Rescue Transponder) are critical devices for locating and directing rescue units in case of abandonment of the ship or severe emergency situations. The correct operation of these devices directly determines the life-saving time in a real emergency. Testing, maintenance and recording discipline is as important as the physical existence of the device.

EPIRB (Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon) is a beacon device that transmits the ship's MMSI and GPS position to Cospas-Sarsat satellites on the 406 MHz frequency, automatically or manually activated when the ship is abandoned. On SOLAS ships, it is mounted outside the bridge, in a quick access bracket, with a hydrostatic release unit (HRU).

It is released at a certain depth with hydrostatic release (HRU) and is automatically activated with water. This section; It covers EPIRB operation and Cospas-Sarsat satellite system, 406 MHz digital identity and GPS location, float-free and HRU mechanism, registration and false alarm management, SOLAS requirement and maintenance/malfunction in engineering depth.

ESP sörveylerinin biriken sonuçları, bir: The accumulated results of ESP surveys determine not only the current class status of a ship but also its long-term economic future. Thickness measurement trends follow a degradation curve over the years; This curve allows predicting when certain structural elements will approach the minimum thickness limit, thus when and to what extent steel renewal will be required. At this point, the shipowner makes a basic economic decision: is it still profitable considering the impending major steel refurbishment expense, the remaining commercial life of the ship and the scrap/second-hand ship prices at the time, or is it more rational to send the ship for dismantling? This calculation is made frequently, especially in bulk carriers and tankers over 15-20 years old; The finding of widespread 'substantial corrosion' revealed in an ESP survey is not an issue that can be solved with a single repair, but may be a signal indicating the end of the economic life of the ship. Therefore, the ESP file is not just an audit trail, it is a basic data set that fleet management uses in asset lifecycle planning.
ESP'nin kapsamı rastgele seçilmemiştir;: The scope of ESP was not chosen randomly; Bulk carriers and tankers are the two ship types where structural failure is most common in ship loss statistics, and there are concrete engineering reasons for this. In bulk carriers, holds are exposed to local stress concentrations created by repeated loading-unloading cycles of high-density solid cargo (mine, coal, grain) and mechanical damage caused by equipment such as grabs/excavators; This accelerates fatigue cracks, especially at hatch bottom corners and transverse bulkheads. In tankers, the problem is chemical: water, hydrogen sulfide and other corrosive components contained in crude oil and its derivatives cause rapid and sometimes unpredictable corrosion, especially on ballast tank upper surfaces and cargo tank steel structures. In both cases, damage accumulates in closed volumes that are invisible to an outside observer and can reach critical levels without warning. Successive bulk carrier losses in the 1990s demonstrated that existing general class surveys were inadequate to capture this type of structural risk, prompting IACS to develop a more frequent and in-depth survey regime specific to these two ship types.
ESP'nin teknik kalbi, geminin çeliğinin: The technical heart of ESP is monitoring how thin the ship's steel becomes over time. Ultrasonic thickness measurement (UTM) is systematically performed in critical structural regions and each measurement is evaluated as part of a trend; When the 'significant' and 'substantial corrosion' thresholds are exceeded, repair or reinforcement becomes necessary. Close-up survey requires the surveyor to physically reach the structural elements inside the tank via scaffolding or rafting (staging/rafting) and closely examine cracks and deformations. The condition of the tank coating and cathodic protection is also evaluated, as coating degradation is a sign of corrosion.
ESP'yi tek seferlik bir denetimden ayıra: What distinguishes ESP from a one-off inspection is that it retains a lifetime structural memory of the ship. ESP file, which must be kept on board; It houses all past survey records, thickness measurement trends and repair history. In this way, the surveyor can make decisions for the future by seeing the rate of deterioration over the years, not the current condition of the ship. The survey scope is planned according to the age and type of the ship; Cleaning and gas-free operations (with closed space entry rules) are required for safe inspection of tanks. Failure to file an ESP on time will result in class suspension, while incomplete filing will result in a PSC finding.

EU ETS denizcilikte kademeli devreye gir: EU ETS phases in for shipping: obligation covers 40% of emissions in 2024, 70% in 2025, 100% from 2026; also, after 2026, methane and nitrous oxide are included in addition to CO₂. The geographical coverage is fine-tuned: the entire emissions of voyages between two EU ports, half of the voyages between an EU port and a non-EU port, the entire time spent at anchor in an EU port are covered. This design aims to limit carbon leakage without exceeding the EU's jurisdiction. Each ship takes as its 'managing authority' the EU state it has visited most in recent years.

EU ETS yıllık bir takvimle işler: yıl bo: The EU ETS operates on an annual schedule: emissions are monitored throughout the year, a certified emissions report is submitted to an independent verifier by 31 March of the following year, and a sufficient number of EUAs are submitted by 30 September. The cost of these obligations is important and charter contracts must clearly state who will pay (shipowner or charterer). Sanctions are harsh: a penalty is paid for each tonne underdelivered, and the quota delivery obligation still remains; Non-compliance lasting more than two years may result in the ship being banned from EU ports (expulsion order). EU ETS, together with FuelEU Maritime in the same scope, constitutes the 'Fit for 55' maritime leg of the EU.
EU ETS, denizciliğe getirilen ilk büyük: The EU ETS is the first major carbon pricing system introduced to shipping and is unique in that it is a non-IMO, regional EU regulation. Its logic is based on the 'polluter pays' principle: a ship must purchase and deliver a market-traded emissions quota (EUA) for every tonne of CO₂ it produces within the EU. Thus, carbon emission is no longer free, but turns into a cost item with a price, and the ship operator is encouraged to avoid this cost by reducing emissions. Eyewall (göz duvarı), gözü çepeçevre sar: Eyewall is the ring consisting of vertically developed cumulonimbus clouds up to 8–15 km high, surrounding the eye and is arguably the most dangerous region of the tropical cyclone. The system's highest sustained winds, strongest gusts, heaviest precipitation, and steepest pressure gradient are found here. Wind speed can jump from near zero to over 100 knots within a few knots as it passes from the calm center of the eye to the eyewall; There is no such sharp transition in any other meteorological system. The barometer can rise or fall at extraordinary rates of 15–20 hPa per hour during eyewall passage. In the Northern Hemisphere, the strongest wind is generally located in the right-front quadrant of the eyewall (relative to the direction of motion of the system); because here the progress speed of the system is added to the rotational wind of the cyclone — this is the micro-scale equivalent of the dangerous semicircle concept. The sea state below the eyewall is beyond definable limits: chaotic waves exceeding 15 meters, visibility reduced to zero due to drifting spray, and the highest values of storm surge in coastal areas are produced in the eyewall region. No commercial ship can maneuver safely in eyewall conditions; The goal of the entire evasion strategy is to keep the ship as far away from this ring as possible.

Eyewall'dan dışa doğru, sistemin dönüş y: Spiral rain bands extend outward from the eyewall, spiraling towards the center in the direction of rotation of the system. Each band; It is like a convective line that carries heavy rain, sudden wind increases (squall), thunderstorms and occasional waterspout/tornado activity. The bands appear on the radar screen as bright arcs bending towards the center, and an experienced observer can roughly estimate the bearing of the cyclone center from the curvature of the bands. In the corridors between the bands, precipitation eases, winds become relatively regulated, and the sky may partially clear; These intervals can create the illusion that the storm is passing amid worsening conditions. However, as the ship approaches the center, the bands become more frequent, the intervals become shorter, and each new band becomes more intense than the previous one. Since wind direction and speed can change within minutes during band crossings, deck operations should not be planned relying on these deceptively calm intervals. In the outermost periphery of the system, high clouds (cirus shield), gradually growing long-period faints and a regular decrease in pressure disrupting the daily tidal oscillation (diurnal variation) are observed; These are classic early signs that a cyclone is approaching while the center is still hundreds of miles away.

FAL Sözleşmesi, bir geminin limanla etki: The FAL Convention standardizes the entire administrative process of a ship's interaction with the port. Before arrival, the ship transmits cargo, crew, dangerous goods and health status information via pre-arrival notification; This allows port and border authorities to prepare in advance. The information that customs, immigration, health and port authorities may request during your stay in the port is limited to the maximum set of documents allowed by the contract; The contract aims to prevent public authorities from requesting unnecessary or repetitive documents. Similarly, formalities are minimized on departure. The main tool of this standardization is the globally recognized FAL forms (General Declaration, Cargo, Stores, Crew Baggage, Crew and Passenger lists, Dangerous Cargo Manifesto); The same data does not have to be prepared again in a different format at each port.
FAL Sözleşmesi, emniyet ya da çevre deği: The FAL Convention is not about safety or the environment; It is the only IMO convention focused on efficiency. Its aim is to minimize, standardize and electronicize as much as possible the documents and formalities required for a ship's entry and exit from the port. Unnecessary paperwork and repetitive notifications both keep the ship waiting in the port and increase the cost of trade. FAL reduces this friction and streamlines international maritime trade by bringing the information that public authorities (customs, border, health, port) may request from the ship into a common form.
FAL'ın çağdaş atılımı, kâğıt formalitele: FAL's contemporary breakthrough is to move paper formalities to electronic data interchange. Maritime Single Window (MSW) ensures that all ship-related notifications are made once and shared with all relevant institutions from a single electronic entry point; This puts an end to the same information being given over and over to different departments and reduces the bureaucracy that keeps the ship waiting in port. The latest revisions also include digital certificate exchange and automation of processes. The Convention also has a humanitarian dimension: regarding stowaways, standard procedures are defined for the detection of stowaways, their accommodation on the ship in humane conditions, sharing of responsibility among flag/port/port of call states, and their repatriation. Thus, FAL observes both efficiency and humane standards while accelerating trade.
FAL'ın en köklü dönüşümü, gemi-liman ver: The most radical transformation of FAL is that it moves ship-port data exchange from paper form to an electronic single window. The Maritime Single Window requirement, adopted with the FAL 13 (2019) amendments and becoming mandatory in all state party ports from 2024, reduces the previously repeated notifications to each public authority (customs, immigration, health, port authority, security) separately and often on paper, to a data set that is entered once from a single digital interface and automatically distributed to all relevant institutions. This change isn't just about saving paper; It also eliminates the risk of inconsistency and delay that occurs when the same information is entered repeatedly in different formats by the agency, Master or owner. The technical backbone of the system is to transport data of standard FAL forms (1-7) with common data models and messaging standards (e.g. UN/EDIFACT-based or XML formatted); Thus, by uploading a single file, a shipping agency can transmit the General Declaration, Cargo Declaration, Crew and Passenger List information to all competent authorities simultaneously. For developing port authorities, this transition is a serious capacity challenge requiring infrastructure investment and staff training; IMO provides support to these countries through technical cooperation programs.
FAL'ın son yıllardaki en önemli atılımı,: FAL's most important breakthrough in recent years is the Maritime Single Window (MSW) obligation: all ship-related notifications are made once, from a single electronic entry point, and shared with all relevant institutions. This puts an end to paper forms and giving the same information over and over to different departments. The latest revisions also include digital certificate exchange and automation of processes. FAL compliance in terms of ship management; It means sending out pre-arrival notifications in a timely manner, integrating into MSW systems, and teaching crews about stowaway procedures.
FAL'ın yedi standart formu, soyut bir be: FAL's seven standard forms are not an abstract list of documents, but a workflow that corresponds exactly to the chronological flow of a port call. In the pre-notification phase before arrival, the ship agency ensures advance preparation of the port, customs and health authorities by transmitting basic information about the ship's ETA, cargo and crew (draft of the General Declaration, Cargo Declaration, Dangerous Cargo Manifesto). On arrival, the General Declaration (FAL 1) formalizes the ship's identity and navigational information, the Crew List (FAL 5) and Passenger List (FAL 6) are submitted to immigration/border control, and the Store Declaration (FAL 3) and Crew Luggage Declaration (FAL 4) are submitted to customs. Changes regarding cargo operations during the stay in port are updated in the Cargo Declaration. On departure, a subset of the documents on arrival is usually resubmitted in an updated form. Keeping the number and content of these documents to a minimum is directly reflected in port efficiency: if a ship waits at the dock or at anchor due to document processing, this means both demurrage-like costs for the shipowner and inefficient use of port capacity. Therefore, FAL's principle of 'no unnecessary or repetitive documents can be requested' is a concrete economic tool that directly shortens port turnaround time.

FSS Code çeşitli söndürme yöntemlerini f: The FSS Code regulates various extinguishing methods for different spaces: fixed CO₂ or foam systems (smothering principle) for high-risk confined spaces such as engine rooms, automatic sprinklers and water mist systems for accommodation spaces, deck foam monitors for cargo areas. In asphyxiating systems such as CO₂, audio/visual warning and time delay are mandatory for people to evacuate. On the detection side, smoke and heat detectors are arranged in zones and loops; The location of a fire can be instantly seen from the panel on the bridge. Manual alarm points initiate human intervention before the automated system catches up.
FSS Code zorunlu hale geldi – yangın güv: FSS Code becomes mandatory – standardization of fire safety systems
FSS Code, her mahallin riskine uygun sab: FSS Code links fixed extinguishing systems to detailed standards appropriate to the risks of each location. For high-risk closed spaces such as engine rooms, fixed gas systems (CO₂ and equivalent) extinguish fire by suffocating oxygen; In these systems, there is an audio/visual warning and a mandatory time delay for people to evacuate, because the gas released into the environment is suffocating for people. Foam systems seal the fuel from the air by covering the surface of the burning liquid with a film layer and are used in engine rooms and tanker decks. Water mist systems provide oxygen dilution through both cooling and evaporation with very small water droplets and have become increasingly common after the halon ban. The code defines the agent quantity, coverage rate, evacuation time, and alarm requirements for each system, along with methods for calculating them.
FSS Code, manuel müdahale araçlarını da: The FSS Code also standardizes the means of manual intervention: fire main, hydrants, hoses and fire pumps of appropriate capacity (including emergency fire pump) and portable extinguishers are available on every ship. Firefighter equipment – self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA), heat-resistant suit, helmet, gloves, lifeline and emergency escape breathing devices (EEBD) – enables the team to get close to the fire. All of these systems remain reliable only with regular testing: the annual weight check of CO₂ cylinders, the weekly function test of alarm panels, the periodic open/close test of fire doors and dampers, the pressure check of SCBA cylinders and the servicing of portable extinguishers cannot be neglected. An undercharged CO₂ system or an inoperative alarm will result in serious deficiency and detention of PSC monitoring; The FSS Code thus forms the technical guarantee of SOLAS Chapter II-2.
FSS Code, SOLAS Chapter II-2'nin 'yangın: FSS Code is SOLAS Chapter II-2's technical answer to the question 'how to fight fire'. A fire on the ship must be taken under control with the ship's resources from the first minutes, since it is impossible to get help from land; Therefore, the design, performance and availability of extinguishing, detection and alarm systems are vital. The code standardizes how each system will be sized, where it will be located, how it will be tested, and how it will be maintained. Thus, the ship's passive protection (structural fire compartments) and active protection (extinguishing systems) establish a defense that complements each other.

FuelEU katı bir yıllık limit dayatmak ye: Rather than imposing a rigid annual limit, FuelEU offers flexibility tools. With compliance balance, the improvement (surplus) made in one year can be transferred to the next year or the deficit can be borrowed. The pooling mechanism allows for exchange between ships: a very clean ship can transfer its surplus as credit to another ship that is substandard; This is a particularly powerful tool in fleet management. FuelEU Maritime ve EU ETS aynı gemileri,: FuelEU Maritime and EU ETS target the same ships, the same voyages and largely the same emissions data, but are not interchangeable; A shipowner must comply with both regulations independently and simultaneously. While the EU ETS generates a cost per carbon because it puts a direct price on emissions, FuelEU places a technical cap on the GHG intensity of the fuel; Even if a ship obtains an EUA and meets its ETS obligation, it will face a separate deficit penalty if it exceeds the FuelEU limit. This dual structure is strategically important as a single compliance tool (e.g. using a biofuel blend) impacts both regulations simultaneously: the biofuel blend both reduces CO₂ burned (hence the need for EUA) and improves the Well-to-Wake density of the fuel (hence FuelEU compliance). So shipowners typically model the costs of the two arrangements together and try to optimize both with a single fuel strategy; A strategy that looks at only one may have an unexpected cost in the other.
FuelEU Maritime, 2025'ten itibaren gemi: FuelEU Maritime sets a target to gradually reduce the GHG intensity of ship fuels from 2025.
FuelEU Maritime, EU ETS ile aynı gemiler: FuelEU Maritime targets the same ships as EU ETS but uses different leverage. While the EU ETS puts a price on emissions, FuelEU puts a direct cap on the greenhouse gas intensity of the energy used by the ship (gCO₂eq/MJ). In other words, instead of 'no matter how much you pollute', it says 'the fuel you use has to be cleaner and cleaner'. This approach forces operators to switch to lower carbon fuels (biofuel, e-fuels, green methanol/ammonia) over time. The two regulations work together: one with a price signal, the other with a standard mandate, pushing for the same decarbonisation target.

FuelEU'nun en ayırt edici yönü Well-to-W: The most distinctive aspect of FuelEU is its Well-to-Wake approach: not only the emissions of the fuel when it is burned on board (Tank-to-Wake), but its entire life cycle emissions from production to transportation are taken into account. This is important because even if a fuel burns cleanly on board, a lot of carbon may have been released in its production; The WtW gaze makes this 'hidden' emission visible. Permissible GHG concentrations gradually tighten from 2025 to 2050 (starting at 2% to 80% reduction). The use of renewable e-fuels (RFNBO) is rewarded with multiplier bonuses, and wind-assisted propulsion systems are also rewarded with benefits.
FuelEU'nun limiti sefer bazlı değil, gem: FuelEU's limit is calculated not on a voyage basis, but on the energy-weighted average of all the energy the ship uses during the calendar year. That is, if the ship used different fuel types (VLSFO, LNG, biofuel blend) in a year, the share of each fuel in the total energy consumption is multiplied by the Well-to-Wake GHG intensity value of that fuel and all contributions are summed to obtain a single average gCO₂eq/MJ value of the ship for that year. This average is compared to the current limit for that year. The practical result of this method is that using clean fuel in one go alone is not enough, what really matters is the total weight of the fuel mixture throughout the year; A ship cannot try to meet the limit by using conventional fuel for most of the year and burning biofuel for a short period at the end of the year, because the low volume clean fuel share will not reduce the annual average sufficiently. This forces the shipowner to plan the use of alternative fuels as a fleet-wide continuous strategy rather than a trip-based tactic.

Gas detectors placed along the bunkering line continuously monitor and give gradual alarms at predefined thresholds; When any leak is detected or the line pressure/temperature is abnormal, the ESD (Emergency Shutdown) system automatically or manually triggers the fuel flow in seconds and quick release couplings are activated. Gelgit (tide), Ay ve Güneş’in yerçekimse:
Tide is the periodic rise and fall of the water level in the oceans and seas due to the gravitational influence of the Moon and the Sun. This effect is astronomically predictable, so tide tables can be calculated long periods in advance. The tide shows different characters around the world: in some ports it rises and falls twice a day (semidiurnal), in others it rises and falls twice a day (diurnal), and in others a mixed cycle is observed.

The importance of tide in terms of maritime is multifaceted: tide information plays a critical role in areas such as port entry-exit timing, UKC (Under Keel Clearance) calculation, under-bridge passage height, coastal passage safety and water surface estimation in rescue operations. It is mandatory for maritime faculty students to know both the physical basis of the tide and the calculation methods from the tables.

Gelgit tabloları (tidal tables), belirli:
Tidal tables give each day's High Water (HW) and Low Water (LW) times and heights for a particular reference port (standard port), usually in UT (UTC) and in meters relative to the chart datum. Admiralty Tide Tables (ATT), publications of the Department of Navigation, Hydrography and Oceanography for Türkiye, and tables of local administrations are among the main sources.

Tide tables are organized in two basic structures: (1) Standard ports: Full annual HW/LW time and heights are given in tabular form. (2) Secondary/subordinate ports: Time and altitude correction factors are given relative to a standard reference port; These factors are applied to the tables of the standard port and the calculation is made for the secondary port.
Gelgit tabloları standart limanlar için: Tide tables give HW/LW times and heights in UT for standard ports.
Gelgit tablolarında spring ve neap arası: In tide tables, the transition between spring and neap can be traced from the systematic increase or decrease in each day's HW/LW height values. In almanacs or annual tables, the correlation between moon phases and tidal amplitude is clearly visible.

If the LAT datum is used, the tide height is always positive or zero (because LAT is the lowest level). If the actual water level had fallen below the LAT, the tide height would have been negative; This is an unusual situation.
Gelgit yüksekliği LAT datum kullanılıyor: Tide height ≥ 0 if LAT datum is used (theoretically can be negative)

Gelgitin ana kaynağı, Ay’ın Dünya üzerin: The main source of tides is the differential gravitational force of the Moon on the Earth. The Moon pulls more strongly on the water mass on the side closer to the Earth; The water swells on this side. On the other hand, a bulge forms on the opposite side of the Earth due to the centrifugal effect (the force resulting from the rotation around the center of gravity of the Earth-Moon system). This is why there are two opposing tidal swells on Earth at the same time.

Its purpose is to measurably detect slow-moving wear, such as corrosion and cracks, before they turn into disasters.

Gemi Aşçısı (Ship's Cook), mürettebatın: The Ship's Cook is the person directly responsible for planning, preparing and serving the crew's three daily main meals and snacks. This responsibility; It includes menu adaptation according to navigation duration and provision stock, consideration of different cultural/religious preferences and dietary restrictions, allergen management, implementation of balanced nutrition principles and service quality. MLC 2006 Regulation 3.2 defines it as the joint obligation of the employer and the cook to provide food on board in sufficient quantity, nutritional value, quality and variety. This section explains step by step the methodology the cook should follow from setting up the menu cycle to serving.

This responsibility; It covers food processing, cold chain control, correct cooking temperatures, cross-contamination prevention, cleaning/disinfection and personal hygiene in accordance with HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) principles. A single foodborne outbreak (e.g. Salmonella, Norovirus) in a closed community can eliminate the entire crew; therefore food safety is part of the operational safety of the ship. This chapter explains the cook's step-by-step process of producing safe food based on HACCP.

Good stock management prevents both food waste and running out of supplies mid-voyage. This section explains the cook's stock cycle step by step.

Gemi belgeleri, denizcilikte \"yapılmamı: Ship documents are the concrete equivalent of the principle in maritime that "if it is not done, it cannot be proven, if it cannot be proven, it is considered not done". The Master's recording and documentation responsibility covers a wide area, ranging from official books such as official log book and deck log book to operational/legal documents such as NOR, Statement of Facts, protest letter, cargo manifest, crew list and stowaway report. The Master's signature on these documents legally binds the ship and the company; It constitutes primary evidence in court, arbitration proceedings and insurance (P&I/H&M) disputes. Gemi Güvenlik Planı (SSP), tanımı gereği: The Ship Security Plan (SSP) is, by definition, a confidential document; because its contents (exact location of access control points, technical details of security equipment, specific steps of alarm procedures) carry information that would directly weaken the ship's defenses in the hands of a malicious actor. This confidentiality differentiates the inspection process from the SMC: rather than reading and confirming every page of the SSP line by line, the PSC or flag state auditor verifies by indirect means that the plan has actually been implemented—by questioning whether the SSO knows the key elements of the plan, testing whether security equipment (SSAS, CCTV, access control) is in working order, reviewing drill logs, and observing physical security arrangements on the ship (lighting, restricted area markings, access points). The SSP's approval also preserves this confidentiality: the plan is approved by the flag state (or competent RSO) and this approval authority comes into play if changes are to be made; The PSC auditor is usually satisfied with confirming that the SSP is approved and that the crew is familiar with its contents, although requesting the plan itself is exceptional and may only be raised in extraordinary circumstances such as security level 3.

Genişleyen kare (expanding square) arama: The expanding square search pattern is one of the most frequently used patterns of IAMSAR and is particularly chosen when there is a single, relatively reliable datum point (last known position or calculated drift position) and a single search instrument is in the field. The logic is simple: the search tool starts from the datum, follows a square spiral that grows from the center outward in perpendicular turns; Each leg extends from the previous one by a certain fixed increment (a distance determined by the scanning range, i.e. the effective viewing/detection width of the vehicle). While this pattern scans the most likely region around the datum first and most intensively, the search expands from the inside out rather than the outside in, gradually reaching surrounding areas where uncertainty increases. The reason why it is preferred is that it offers both simplicity of application (single vehicle, navigation with simple turn commands) and the most efficient coverage rate in scenarios where datum reliability is high and drift uncertainty is low. If datum uncertainty is high or there is more than one asset, patterns that cover a larger area or are suitable for multi-vehicle coordination, such as parallel track or sector search, are preferred instead; This choice is the OSC's first tactical decision based on the conditions on the ground.

EVDI, on the other hand, is not a compliance threshold, but a ranking commercial rating (from A to G) and does not have any legal sanction. GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) is an international system that standardizes maritime distress and safety communications on a global scale and has been fully in force since 1999. GMDSS; It covers the functions of giving and receiving distress alarms, search and rescue coordination, broadcasting navigational and meteorological safety information, and general communication between ships and between ships and shores. The basis of the system lies in the sea area classification, and this classification directly determines the communication equipment to be carried on the ship.

GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) is a mandatory global communication system required by SOLAS, which guarantees the ship's automatic and rapid communication with coastal search and rescue (SAR) and nearby ships in case of distress. The basic logic of the system is not "what to look for" but "which equipment in which sea area" approach. This section; It covers the basic functions of GMDSS (distress alerting, SAR coordination, MSI), sea area definitions (A1-A4) and equipment requirements for each area, DSC logic, MSI publications (NAVTEX/SafetyNET), redundancy/power requirements and maintenance/certification in engineering depth.

Area A1 is the area under DSC (Digital Selective Calling) coverage of at least one VHF shore station; its typical range is 20–30 nautical miles. Göz (eye), olgunlaşmış bir tropikal sikl: The eye is the approximately circular calm region located at the center of rotation of a mature tropical cyclone. Its typical diameter is between 20–60 km; However, 'pinhole' eyes that can narrow down to 8–10 km in very intense, compact systems and eyes that exceed 100 km in weak or very wide systems have also been observed. As a general rule, a small and sharply circumscribed eye indicates a concentrated and violent system. Within the eye, surface wind often drops below 10–15 knots, precipitation ceases, and the sky may partially or completely clear; The stars can be seen at night and the sun can be seen during the day. The lowest pressure of the system at sea level is measured at the center of the eye; In severe hurricanes, this value drops below 950 hPa and in record systems, it drops below 900 hPa. The eye is also the 'warm core' of the system: due to the compressive heating of the collapsing air, the inside of the eye is at intermediate levels 5–10°C warmer than the surrounding atmosphere at the same altitude. This warm core is the key thermodynamic feature that distinguishes tropical cyclones from mid-latitude low pressures (cold core systems). When looked up from inside the eye, the eyewall clouds appear like a giant stadium tribune rising all around, which is called the 'stadium effect'.

Gözün açık ve sıcak olmasının temel nede: What is the main reason why the eye is open and warm?
Gözün en sinsi tehlikesi, atmosferdeki s: The most insidious danger to the eye is that the calmness in the atmosphere is not reflected in the sea. Even if the wind calms down, the sea inside the eye is in a completely chaotic 'confused/pyramidal sea' state, formed by the convergence of waves produced from all directions of the system to the center. Sequences of waves coming from different directions overlap, producing pyramidal, steep and unpredictable waves; It is impossible to predict the wave direction because there is no wind to regulate the waves. These conditions make the ship's rolling and pitching movements unsynchronized and unpredictable; A favorable environment is created for dangerous dynamic stability events, including parametric roll. Many ships throughout history have been injured in the eye or were caught unprepared for the second half of the storm, thinking that the wind had stopped and the storm was over. The critical fact is this: during eye passage, the wind returns from the OPPOSITE direction before entering. If the diameter of the eye is 30 km and the forward speed of the system is 15 knots, the calm period may last only 30–60 minutes; then the opposite side eyewall comes in full intensity with no gradual increase. The barometer reads its lowest value during this transition; The lowest reading means 'the center is above us', not 'danger is over'.
Gözün karanlığa uyumunun korunması ve dı: To protect the eye's adaptation to the dark and to see outside
Gözün Tanımı ve Fiziksel Özellikleri: Definition and Physical Characteristics of the Eye
Gözün varlığı iki temel fiziksel mekaniz: The existence of the eye is the result of two basic physical mechanisms. The first is dynamic balance: the air flowing spirally towards the center of the cyclone gradually accelerates as it approaches the center due to the conservation of angular momentum (like an ice skater accelerating when he gathers his arms). At a certain radius, the centrifugal force balances the pressure gradient force pulling the air in, and the air cannot be brought any further into the center; This balance radius determines the inner boundary of the eyewall and therefore the size of the eye. All the moist air flowing in is forced to rise violently above this ring—this is how the eyewall's giant cumulonimbus tower is fed. The second mechanism is related to subsidence: some of the air that rises within the eyewall and discharges outwards at the top returns to the eye and collapses downwards there. The collapsing air is compressed and heated adiabatically; The relative humidity of the heated air decreases, clouds dissolve and the sky clears. This is why the eye is both open and warm. The eye becomes apparent on satellite and radar images as the system exceeds tropical storm strength and begins to mature (usually as sustained winds approach 64 knots); The emergence of a clear and symmetrical eye is one of the most reliable signs that the system is strengthened.

GPS (Global Positioning System), Amerika:
GPS (Global Positioning System) is a space-based satellite navigation system developed by the American Department of Defense and opened to full capacity for civilian use since 1995. The system consists of at least 24 active satellites positioned in various orbits around the Earth, and these satellites constantly emit strong time signals. A receiver on Earth calculates its own position by receiving these signals.

The revolutionary importance of GPS in terms of maritime is that it offers continuous, automatic and high-accuracy position determination. GPS works day and night, in all weather conditions, in every ocean; The sextant has become a complement to radar and visual positioning and has become the primary data source of modern ECDIS systems.

However, GPS also carries the danger of blind trust. Interrupting, jamming or spoofing the signal coming from satellites can disable GNSS systems or cause incorrect position indication. Therefore, STCW and IMO define GPS as a supporting tool; navigators must maintain radar, astronomy and conventional positioning proficiency.

GPS alıcısı, her uydunun göndermekte old: The GPS receiver measures the time difference between the signal sent by each satellite and the copy signal produced by the receiver itself. This time difference is multiplied by the speed of light to calculate the distance to the satellite (pseudo-range). The term 'pseudo' indicates that the error in the receiver clock adds error to the distance.

Satellite clock and orbit errors, atmospheric delays (ionosphere/troposphere), receiver clock error, multipath reflection and receiver noise magnify the total error. At moments when the satellite geometry is weak (high DOP), the same error size produces larger deviations in position.

GPS’te trilaterasyon uygulaması şöyle iş: Trilateration in GPS works like this: each satellite broadcasts a message containing its position and signal sending time. When the receiver receives this signal, it calculates the pseudo-range to the satellite by multiplying the signal delay (Δt) by the speed of light (c). This so-called distance defines the sphere surface and indicates that the receiver is located somewhere on this sphere. The intersection of 3 spheres obtained with 3 satellites theoretically gives two points; The point outside the earth is automatically eliminated and the 3D location is obtained.

Grain Code, dökme tahılın kendine özgü b: The Grain Code addresses a unique hazard of bulk grain: the grain behaves like a fluid and shifts to one side in the hold when the ship heels. After loading, the grain settles a bit, leaving space at the top; When the ship lurches, the grain sliding into this gap moves the center of gravity to one side and causes the ship to take a permanent heel to that side. This tendency disrupts balance and can lead to the risk of capsizing in overlapping rolls. The code aims to calculate this shear moment and ensure that the ship still has sufficient stability.

Grain Code'un teknik özü, tahıl kaymasın: The technical essence of the Grain Code is to calculate the heeling moment resulting from grain shifting and prove that the ship's stability reserve is sufficient for this. The calculation uses a volumetric method based on bin geometry: in fully filled bins, it is assumed that the grain will shift towards the upper space at a certain angle (by default, approximately 15°) after settling, while in partially filled bins, a larger shift (approximately 25°) is possible. These assumed shifts produce an overturning moment for each hold, and the total moment is compared to the ship's stability curve. Partially full cargo holds are therefore the riskiest; Filling as fully as possible and smooth trimming is preferred. The ship's approved grain loading booklet contains these calculations for different loading situations and the Master makes the loading plan accordingly.

Grup A yüklerde, nem belirli bir eşiği a: In Group A loads, if the humidity exceeds a certain threshold, the load changes from solid to fluid behavior (liquefaction) due to the vibration and movement of the ship. The fluidized load may slide to one side, causing a sudden and dangerous collapse, or even capsizing. To prevent this, the moisture content of the load must be below the Transportable Moisture Limit (TML) value. TML is usually determined as 90% of the Flow Moisture Point. If in doubt the Master may carry out a simple field check such as a 'can test', but the official decision is based on the laboratory certificate. If the humidity exceeds the TML, the load is rejected.
Grup A yükleri için kodun en önemli sayı: The code's most important numerical concept for Group A loads is the Transportable Moisture Limit (TML): the maximum moisture content at which the load can be safely transported, typically set at 90% of the flow moisture point (FMP). The actual moisture content of the load must be below this limit. Laboratory tests (Proctor/Fagerberg, flow table) and a rapid 'can/should test' in the field are used to confirm this. The loader must provide the ship with a cargo declaration containing TML and actual humidity values; Group A cargo should not be accepted without this document or without a moisture test.
Grup A yüklerinin güvenli taşınması, nem: Safe transportation of Group A loads relies on humidity control. The actual humidity of the cargo must be below the Transportable Humidity Limit (TML); TML is generally determined as 90% of the Flow Moisture Point (FMP). FMP is the moisture threshold at which the load changes from solid to fluid behavior. Accredited laboratory tests are used to determine these values: Methods such as Proctor/Fagerberg test, flow table test and penetration test are suitable for different load types. A 'can test' (putting the sample in a container and tamping it) can be done in the field as a quick preliminary check, but it is not a substitute for laboratory testing. The loader must provide the ship with a signed cargo information form (cargo declaration) containing TML and actual humidity values, and this document and the tests must date at most a certain number of days ago; otherwise the load is rejected.

For example, the 500 GT threshold introduces many of SOLAS' certification requirements for cargo ships (such as Safety Construction, Safety Equipment) and the ISM Code's mandatory SMC/DOC regime; While a ship of 499 GT remains exempt from this heavy certification and management system burden, a ship reaching 500 GT faces many new statutory obligations at the same time. A similar break is seen in the MLC Certificate requirement. This sharp threshold effect can become a conscious engineering goal for ship designers and shipowners: in this approach, known as 'tonnage optimisation', the internal volume of a ship is designed to be kept below the threshold without significantly sacrificing capacity – for example, by leaving certain above-deck areas partially open or creating voids that are not included in the volume calculation. This practice is sometimes criticized by regulatory authorities because it can create a mismatch between the ship's actual carrying capacity and the safety and labor standards regime to which it is subject; The IMO and some flag states have reviewed their tonnage calculation rules from time to time in order to limit such 'threshold gaming'.

Güvenlik seviyeleri arasındaki geçiş, kâ: The transition between security levels is not just a classification on paper; Triggers visible tangible changes on the ship. Level 1 (normal) covers permanent minimum measures: control of access points, random patrol on deck, entry to the ship with ID check. When moving to Level 2 (escalated), access control is tightened, typically in response to regional threat intelligence or a specific incident: additional personnel are assigned to the gangway, visitor and cargo checks are conducted more frequently and in greater detail, entries into restricted areas are recorded, the frequency of night patrols is increased, and security information sharing with neighboring ships/port facility is intensified. Transition to Level 3 (extraordinary) refers to urgent measures taken against a concrete and imminent threat: cargo operations may be stopped, access to the ship may be completely restricted or limited to authorized security personnel only, coordinated evacuation with the port facility or port departure scenarios may be activated. At each level transition, a Declaration of Security (DoS) is expected to be signed between the SSO, CSO and PFSO and the implemented measures are recorded.

Training Record Book (TRB) is the official document of this process.

Intern; Observes radar/ARPA, ECDIS, AIS and other bridge devices, practices position determination and plotting, learns COLREG rules in the field and gets used to keeping a deck logbook. The intern does not have the authority to independently approve plans; Everything he prepares is checked by the Second Officer and the Master. This section explains in detail how the trainee will contribute to navigation planning, what resources to use, and what mistakes to avoid.

The trainee never participates in these tasks as an independent responsible person, but under the direct supervision of a deck officer or experienced crew member. The aim at this stage is to identify the main route corridor and avoid major obstacles. Large-scale charts are used during the coastal approach, strait passage, narrow water navigation and harbor maneuver phases. These charts make it possible to manage shoals, restricted areas, sectoral lights and buoy arrays that are directly related to the draft of the ship.

In this expression, as the denominator decreases, the scale increases and the detail increases; As the denominator increases, the scale decreases and the detail decreases. In maritime, a large-scale chart is a chart with a numerically small denominator. Harbor charts are therefore large scale; Offshore charts are small scale.

For this reason, distance measurement, position marking and route correction should be done on the largest scale chart possible. The same principle applies to route measurement; An error of a few degrees, which seems insignificant on a small scale, can carry the ship out of the channel on a large scale.

Harmonized Survey System (HSS), farklı s: Harmonized Survey System (HSS) combines surveys required by different conventions (SOLAS, MARPOL, Load Line) in a common schedule; This is to prevent a ship from being constantly interrupted by independent surveys at different times of the year. Annual surveys may be conducted within a ±3 month window around the anniversary of the certificate; This flexibility ensures that the ship can meet the surveyor regardless of which port or operation it is in at that time. The interim survey is scheduled for the second to third year, the renewal survey for the end of the fifth year, and the renewal window carries a similar tolerance (usually 3 months before – 3 months after). This window system is not pure bureaucracy for the shipowner, but a concrete operational planning tool: charter contracts, dry dock appointments and crew changes are arranged according to these windows, since a survey outside the window effectively invalidates the certificate and subjects the ship to docking or PSC detention. That's why operations departments treat the survey schedule as an integral input into route planning.

Head-on (karşılıklı yaklaşma) durumu, CO: The head-on situation necessitates one of COLREG's clearest and most uncontroversial maneuvers: both motor ships turn to starboard (right) and pass each other's starboard side. Rule 14 is the only rule that is symmetrical — placing equal obligations on both ships. The contribution of the head-on scenario is high in collision cases analyzed around the world; The main reasons for this include visibility restriction due to fog or nights, errors in ARPA interpretation, and uncertainty on the border between head-on and crossing. Common errors arising from maneuvering are: (1) ships turning in different directions — if one turns to starboard and the other to port, the distance is closed; (2) small steering changes — a change of 5° is not noticed by the opposing ship and a head and shoulders effect is created by crossing; (3) Making illegal agreements such as 'port to port' over VHF. According to IMO guidelines, only Rule 14 should apply; Querying 'to which side' over VHF cannot replace COLREG as it increases the risk in case of communication failure.

For EU-flagged ships, this is directly the flag state; For non-EU flagged ships, the determination is made according to the member state that the ship visited the most EU ports in the previous four monitoring periods and is announced in the list published by the Commission. If a ship has never called at an EU port or if the data is insufficient, the first member state it called is considered the authority for that period. In practice, this means that the administrative point of contact from which the shipowner will have the MRV monitoring plan approved, select the verifying body and receive the Document of Compliance may vary, so the fleet manager must follow which authority applies to each ship and that authority's national implementing practices (language, portal, time tolerances). IAPP is the bridge from classical pollution control to climate regulation. SEEMP (Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan), which is mandatory to be kept on board, has three parts: general efficiency management (Part I), IMO DCS data collection plan (Part II) and CII management plan (Part III). Thus, under the IAPP certificate, both the ship's design efficiency (EEXI) and operational carbon performance (CII) are monitored. The scope of the certificate has expanded over time: fuel or scrubber verification for sulfur (SOx) compliance, registration of ozone depleting substances (ODS – halon, CFC), VOC management plan for crude oil tankers and approved ship incinerators are also evaluated under this certificate. Missing NOx file, SOx incompatibility, or SEEMP deficiency leads to PSC deficiency and possible detention; Without the certificate, the ship cannot make international voyages.
IAPP'nin en teknik unsuru, gemideki 130: The most technical element of the IAPP is the NOx Technical File for each diesel engine above 130 kW on board. This file documents that the engine's nitrogen oxide emissions comply with the Tier I, II or III limits applied depending on the year of manufacture and cruising region, and identifies all 'adjustable components' (injector, fuel pump timing, turbocharger, valve adjustment) that affect the engine's emissions. The important thing is that the maintenance of the engine is kept within the approved parameters in this file: if the emission characteristic of the engine is changed during a maintenance or parts replacement, this must be re-verified by an approved method (e.g. onboard monitoring or parameter control). Tier III applies only in NOx Emission Control Areas (NECA) and usually requires additional technology such as selective catalytic reduction (SCR) or exhaust gas recirculation (EGR). If the file is not up-to-date, it will cause a deficiency in the PSC.
IAPP'nin teknik kalbi iki ana kirleticid: The technical heart of IAPP is two main pollutants. On the NOx side, every diesel engine above 130 kW has a NOx Technical Dossier and is subject to Tier I, II or (in NECA regions) Tier III limits depending on the year of engine manufacture; Engine maintenance (injector, turbocharger, timing) directly affects this harmony. On the SOx side, compliance is achieved with either low sulfur fuel or an approved scrubber and is documented with BDNs and fuel samples. Over time, the scope of this certification has expanded: ODS registrations, VOC management plan for crude oil tankers, approved ship burners and from 2023 EEXI verification have also been added to the IAPP.

IBC Code, dökme tehlikeli kimyasal taşıy: IBC Code is based on the principle of designing ships carrying bulk hazardous chemicals according to the risk posed by the cargo. The logic is this: the more dangerous the substance transported (toxicity, flammability, environmental damage), the higher the survivability of the ship should be. Therefore, ships are classified as Types 1, 2 and 3; Type 1 carries the most hazardous loads and is subject to the most stringent subdivision, damage stability and tank layout requirements (tanks furthest outside the hull, limited in volume). Thus, the damage that the most dangerous cargo may cause to the environment and the ship in the event of a collision or grounding is minimized.
IBC Code, SDS, Certificate of Fitness, P: The category, toxicity, flash point, vapor pressure, reactivity, heating, inerting, inhibitor and special equipment conditions of the product are verified from the IBC Code, SDS, Certificate of Fitness, P&A Manual and charterer instructions. Tank coating compatibility list is checked. Reactive products are not only in the tank; It is also divided into common line, vent, slop and tank cleaning systems.
IBC Code'un tasarım mantığı, geminin hay: The design logic of the IBC Code is to determine the survivability of the ship according to the danger of the cargo it carries. Type 1 ships carry the most dangerous cargoes and are subject to the most stringent requirements: their tanks are located furthest from the hull, their volume is limited, and damage stability criteria are the strictest; The aim is to minimize the likelihood of spilling the most dangerous cargo in a collision or grounding. Type 2 and Type 3 ships have gradually relaxed requirements for less hazardous cargo. Each cargo is identified with the minimum ship type it requires in the list in Chapter 17; A ship can only carry products authorized in its certificate (Certificate of Fitness) and only if the ship type conditions they require are met. Partitioning, double skin and damage stability calculations form the basis of this classification.
IBC Code'un Tip 1/2/3 ayrımı soyut bir e: The IBC Code's Type 1/2/3 distinction is not an abstract labeling, but an engineering rule with direct geometric and volumetric consequences. The type of ship required for the transportation of a substance is determined in the list in Chapter 17 according to the seriousness of the damage that that substance may cause to the environment and human health in an accident; toxicity, flammability, corrosivity and reactivity are the inputs to this assessment. For the most dangerous cargoes that must be carried in Type 1, the minimum distance of the cargo tank to the ship's shell and collision bulkhead is kept as wide as possible; This reduces the possibility of the tank being punctured in the event of a side collision or grounding impact to the bow area. By the same logic, the maximum volume that a single tank can carry in Type 1 ships is strictly limited (approximately 1250 m³), because the amount that can be spilled in case of damage is kept under control with this upper limit. In Type 2 ships, distance and volume requirements are gradually relaxed, while in Type 3 they are relatively least restrictive. This triple system allows cargo of different hazard levels to be carried together within the same ship hull, but each with physical protection appropriate to its own risk level.

IGC Code, kargo tanklarını taşıdıkları b: The IGC Code classifies cargo tanks according to the pressure/temperature regime they carry and leak management philosophy. Self-contained tanks are of three subtypes: Type C is designed as a pressure vessel and generally does not require a secondary barrier (common on LPG and ethylene vessels); Types A and B are suitable for lower pressure, larger volume, cryogenic loads and require a secondary barrier (Type B partial, Type A full secondary barrier). Membrane tanks (GTT Mark III, NO96) are a thin system of barrier and insulation layers supported by the ship's hull and are standard on large LNG carriers. Material selection is critical in cryogenic conditions: ordinary steel becomes brittle in extreme cold, so special low-temperature steels, nickel alloys or stainless steel are used on surfaces in contact with the cargo. The tank type also determines the ship's overall damage stability and layout design.
IGC Code, LNG, LPG, etilen ve amonyak gi: The IGC Code governs the unique hazards of tankers carrying liquefied gases such as LNG, LPG, ethylene and ammonia. These cargoes are kept in liquid form either at very low temperature (cryogenic, approximately -163°C for LNG) or under high pressure; When they leak, they can expand rapidly and form flammable or toxic clouds, and their extreme cold can make the steel hull brittle. The Code designs these ships to the highest technical standards, making gas tankers the most sophisticated and tightly regulated ships at sea. The main purpose is to keep the cargo under control under all circumstances and isolated from areas where people are present.
IGC tank types: A (full secondary barrie: IGC tank types: A (full secondary barrier), B (partial), C (pressurized, no barrier), membrane (LNG)
IGC'nin teknik kalbi kargo tankı tasarım: The technical heart of the IGC is the cargo tank design. Tanks can be freestanding (type A, B, C), membrane or integral; Each type is based on a different pressure/temperature and leak management philosophy. The critical concept is the secondary barrier: if the primary tank leaks, there is a second layer of protection to prevent cold liquid from reaching the ship's hull and brittle it. The interbarrier space is constantly monitored for temperature and gas, so that the slightest leak is detected early. The design of membrane tanks (GTT Mark III, NO96) is the most advanced example of this double protection principle.
IGC'nin temel emniyet ilkesi, soğuk karg: IGC's basic safety principle is that refrigerated cargo should not reach the ship's hull under any circumstances; because a cryogenic leak can instantly embrittle the steel and lead to structural collapse. Therefore, a secondary barrier is envisaged that is activated in case the primary tank leaks, and this barrier must be able to safely hold the leaking liquid for a certain period of time. The interbarrier space between the primary and secondary barrier and the surrounding spaces are constantly monitored for temperature and gas; A sudden temperature drop or gas detection gives early warning of even the slightest leak. This monitoring network is an integral part of the cargo control system and allows the crew to respond to a problem before it becomes a disaster.
IGF Code kapsamında gaz yakıtlı gemi eği: Adding gas fueled ship training within the scope of IGF Code
IGF Code yakıt gaz sisteminin tasarım ve: The IGF Code regulates the design and operation of the fuel gas system.
IGF Code, gaz yakıtın gemide depolanması: The IGF Code binds the storage and distribution of gaseous fuel on board to detailed technical requirements. LNG is generally kept at cryogenic temperature in insulated Type C pressure tanks; The tank layout is positioned at a certain distance from the hull so that it will not be damaged in collision and grounding. The fuel preparation room and fuel valve units (TVU/GVU) in the engine room control the pressure and temperature of the gas. The bunkering station ensures fuel intake from a safe point, with leak collection and emergency separation mechanisms. All these systems are designed on the 'double barrier' principle: at each point where the gas is captured, there are two independent layers of protection (e.g. double-walled pipe and ventilated enclosure) to ensure that even in the event of a single fault, the gas does not reach occupied areas.
IGF Code, geleneksel SOLAS bölümlerinin: The IGF Code deliberately departs from the 'prescriptive' approach seen in most traditional SOLAS chapters, as gaseous fuel technologies can be implemented in different arrangements on each ship and prescribing a single standard design restricts innovation. Instead, 'alternative designs and regulations' are opened for fuels or regulations that are outside Part A-1 and do not yet have a detailed prescription: the designer must prove through risk analysis that the solution he proposes is at least as safe as the prescribed standard. The process typically begins with a HAZID (Hazard Identification) study; Here, possible hazard scenarios at each stage of design (storage, pipeline, bunkering, emergency) are systematically listed. Then, HAZOP (Hazard and Operability Study) is performed for critical scenarios; In this study, each system element is questioned with 'deviation words' (more, less, none, reverse) and failure chains and their consequences are detailed. The output of these analyzes is evaluated by an independent third party (usually a classification society) and presented to management; Approval is a formal decision that the documented risk level of the design is acceptable. This process ensures that the design for each new fuel, from LNG to ammonia, is shaped by real-world failure probabilities.
IGF Code, gemilerin geleneksel fuel oil: The IGF Code was established to manage new risks arising as ships switch from conventional fuel oil to LNG and other low flash point fuels. These fuels have an environmental advantage but are a safety challenge: when leaked as a gas, it spreads rapidly, is stored at very low temperatures, and forms an explosive mixture in a narrow range. The distinctive approach of the code is that it is goal-based rather than writing every detail in advance: the designer must prove the security of the system through structured risk analysis such as HAZID/HAZOP and obtain administration/class approval. This flexibility allows nascent fuel technologies to develop safely.
IGF Code'un ayırt edici yönü, her ayrınt: The distinguishing aspect of the IGF Code is that it is goal-based and risk-based, rather than prescribing every detail. The designer must prove the security of the system through structured risk analyzes such as HAZID and HAZOP and obtain administration/class approval; This flexibility allows nascent fuel technologies to develop safely. Although the code currently covers LNG predominantly, new fuels are coming into focus with decarbonisation: interim guidelines are in place for methanol, requirements are being developed for ammonia (which presents additional challenges due to its toxicity) and hydrogen. Each new fuel brings unique hazards (flash point, toxicity, flame speed, storage temperature) and the IGF's risk-based framework is the way to manage this diversity. Crews are required to receive special gas fuel training under STCW.
IGF'nin temel mühendislik felsefesi 'çif: IGF's core engineering philosophy is 'double barrier': at each point where the fuel is held there are two independent layers of protection to ensure that even in the event of a single fault, the gas does not reach occupied areas. Fuel tanks, pipelines and connections are designed with this logic; Double-walled pipes and vented casings are used to catch and safely expel gas leaks. The engine room is divided into 'gas safe' and 'gas dangerous' zones; Electrical equipment is selected in accordance with this classification. Gas detection systems constantly monitor and when the threshold is exceeded, automatic emergency shutdown (ESD) is activated and immediately cuts off the fuel flow.

II-1, geminin su altı bütünlüğünü çok ka: II-1 secures the ship's underwater integrity in a multi-layered manner. The principle of subdivision divides the ship into compartments with watertight bulkheads; the aim is for the ship to remain afloat and stable when one or more compartments take on water. For passenger and cargo ships after 2009, the probabilistic damage stability method (required A index ≥ reached A index) is used, which evaluates damage scenarios together with their probabilities. Section; Covers type and closing times of watertight doors, double bottom requirements, damage control plans and bilge/ballast pumping arrangements. On the machinery and electrical side, it regulates the redundancy of main and auxiliary engines, emergency power sources (emergency generator), steering gear (main and auxiliary system, test requirements) and rudder control; The aim is to ensure that a single malfunction does not render the ship unmanageable.

II-2, yangını üç stratejiyle ele alır: ö: II-2 addresses fire with three strategies: prevention, containment, and suppression. Prevention; This is achieved through the restriction of flammable materials, safe design of fuel/oil systems and control of ignition sources. Containment delays the spread of fire in one space to neighboring spaces by dividing the ship into main vertical zones with class A and B fire compartments (different endurance times from A-60 to A-0); Fire doors, dampers and emergency stop of ventilation complete this system. Perception; It instantly determines the location of the fire with smoke and heat detectors, manual alarm points and central panels on the bridge. Suppression varies by space: constant CO₂/foam/water mist for engine room, sprinklers for accommodation spaces, foam monitors for deck. The chapter also regulates the design of escape routes, emergency lighting, firefighter equipment (SCBA, EEBD) and additional measures specific to tankers (inert gas, foam).
III, kazadan sonra hayatta kalmayı hem d: III regulates survival after the accident, both in terms of equipment and organization. On the equipment side, survival craft (fully enclosed, free-falling lifeboats, liferafts), rescue boat, lowering devices (davit) and personal equipment (life jacket, immersion suit, TPA) are determined in terms of number and performance; Marine Evacuation System (MES) is prescribed for rapid evacuation on passenger ships. On the organizational side, it is mandatory for each ship to have a muster list (fire chart), each crew member must know their duty in the event of an emergency, and muster stations must be marked. Drills are the heart of this section: abandon ship and fire drills are carried out at regular intervals, lifeboat launches are carried out and recorded at regular intervals; Familiarization training is given to newly joined personnel. The detail of technical standards is left to the LSA Code.

The segregation table and special provisions determine which items should be kept side by side and which should be kept separately. The stacking plan is made according to these rules; below/above deck, distance from heat sources and ventilation are also taken into account. An incorrect separation may cause two individually harmless loads to combine and produce fire or toxic gas.
IMDG'nin en hayati operasyonel bölümü, b: The most vital operational part of IMDG is segregation rules, which prevent substances that may react dangerously with each other from being transported together. The segregation table determines which classes will be 'kept out', 'segregated', 'separated one bay/hatch apart' or 'separated one bay apart'; For example, acids and cyanides, oxidizers and flammables must be kept at certain distances, otherwise two harmless charges may combine and produce fire or poisonous gas. Stowage rules regulate whether each item should be carried above or below deck, how far away from heat sources and living quarters it should be carried, and what ventilation conditions are required. Safe packaging of containers and vehicles is coordinated with CTU Code, and lashing during transportation is coordinated with CSS Code.

IMO 2020 olarak anılan düzenleme, gemi y: The regulation, referred to as IMO 2020, triggered one of the largest fuel transitions in maritime history by reducing the sulfur content in ship fuel from 3.50% to 0.50% on a global scale. Its purpose is human health and the environment: when burned, sulfur in fuel forms sulfur oxides (SOx) and fine particulate matter; these lead to acid rain, respiratory diseases and premature deaths. The regulation imposes a global cap of 0.50% for the rest of the world, alongside the 0.10% limit already in force in the Emission Control Areas (ECA – Baltic, North Sea, North America). There will be SOx ECA in the Mediterranean in 2028.

The sector is responsible for approximately 2.5-3% of global CO₂ and continues to grow; Therefore, this strategy was created as the maritime equivalent of the Paris Agreement targets. IMO Resolution A.893(21) came into force in 1999 under the title 'Guidelines for Voyage Planning' and sets out the voyage planning standards that should be applied on all ships operating international voyages. The decision divides navigation planning into four mandatory phases: Appraisal, Planning, Execution and Monitoring. These four stages ensure that the ship operates within a structured safety framework at every step from departure to arrival.

IMO A.893(21) becomes a legal obligation when considered together with SOLAS Chapter V Rule 34. SOLAS V/34 requires appropriate navigation planning to 'plan the journey and expectations in advance'. The application of these two regulations together defines passage planning as both a technical and legal obligation.

IMO, egzoz gazı temizleme sistemlerini (: Although IMO has approved exhaust gas cleaning systems (EGCS) under guidance MEPC.259(68), this global approval does not mean that every port or coastal state will accept open circuit washwater discharge. The open circuit scrubber washes the sulfur compounds in the exhaust gas directly with sea water and discharges the acidified, heavy metal and PAH-containing water into the sea; While this may be considered acceptable in the open ocean when the dilution capacity is high, it raises local pollution concentration concerns in closed harbor basins, bottlenecks, or waters with sensitive ecosystems. For this reason, some countries and ports have partially or completely banned open circuit discharge (in their territorial waters or within port borders). As a result, a ship with an open-circuit scrubber must check in advance in its voyage planning which ports or regions allow open-circuit discharge, switch to closed-loop mode in prohibited areas (in hybrid systems) or switch to compatible low-sulfur fuel in that region; This limits the expected operational flexibility of the scrubber investment to regional constraints.

IMSBC Code'un pratik omurgası, 350'den f: The practical backbone of the IMSBC Code is load profiles (schedules) prepared separately for more than 350 bulk cargoes. Each profile; It includes the load description, group, stowing factor, hazards during transportation, ventilation and gas measurement requirements, loading/unloading precautions and emergency procedures. If a new cargo that is not listed is to be transported, a temporary transport permit must be obtained from the competent authorities. Trimming (even distribution of the load within the hold) is essential for both stability and structural load distribution; It is especially critical for liquefiable loads and to prevent structural stress. The loading operation is coordinated with BLU Code, which standardizes the communication and loading plan between the ship and the terminal; Unbalanced or too rapid loading can impose harmful bending/torsional stress on the hull, so the loading order and rate are monitored by a loading computer.
IMSBC Code'un tüm sınıflandırması üç gru: The entire classification of the IMSBC Code is built around three groups, with each group representing a different philosophy of hazards. Group A are cargoes that can liquefaction when containing moisture; The main risk is sudden loss of balance. Group B is cargo carrying chemical hazards; They can start a fire, deplete oxygen and suffocate the hold, emit toxic or flammable gas, or react dangerously with water/air. Group C are relatively harmless loads that neither liquefy nor pose chemical hazards (but even these can present risks such as structural overloading and dust). Some loads show both A and B properties (A&B). Knowing which group a load is in determines all the precautions to be taken (whether ventilation is open or closed, whether gas measurement is required, whether humidity testing is required); That's why group confirmation before loading is the critical first step.
IMSBC Code'un varlık nedeni, dökme katı: The raison d'être of the IMSBC Code is the deadly risks behind the innocent appearance of bulk solid cargoes. The most critical danger is liquefaction: fine-grained cargoes containing moisture (nickel ore, bauxite, some concentrates) can suddenly begin to behave like a liquid with the vibration and movement of the ship. In this case, the cargo slides in the hold, disrupts the ship's heeling balance and may cause capsizing within minutes. The code divides cargo into three groups according to their hazard characteristics: Group A is liquefiable cargo, Group B is those that carry chemical hazards (fire, poisonous gas, oxygen consumption), and Group C is those that do not carry both risks.

The IMSBC Code differs from neighboring codes in terms of its scope: grain, with a separate Grain Code because it is at risk of shifting rather than liquefying; Packaged dangerous goods are regulated by IMDG Code.
