In-Water Survey (IWS), belirli koşullard: Although In-Water Survey (IWS) makes it possible to delay the need for a dry dock in certain conditions, it does not offer a true inspection alternative for some components because accurate assessment of these components requires complete drainage of water and direct access. Rudder pintle wear requires micron-level tolerance measurements that cannot be measured with the tactile sensitivity of the diver or ROV; This measurement is only reliable when the wake is taken out of the water and measured mechanically. Sea chest screens require visual and physical inspection for fouling and corrosion accumulated on the interior surface, underwater turbidity and access angle severely limit this inspection. The bow thruster tunnel and the propeller-bearing system inside it, as well as sensitive electronic casings such as the sonar dome, should similarly be examined outside the water, with direct view, and if necessary, by dismantling them. That is why the classification rules always define IWS as a 'conditional' alternative: ships meeting certain age, history and condition criteria are permitted for a limited number of successive periods, but in the case of these components the scope of IWS is either reduced or a dry dock is required directly.

Australia's AMSA and South Africa's SAMSA are known for their stringent practices and focus areas (e.g. structural integrity, MLC, environmental compliance); Ships entering the ports of these countries must meet these national expectations as well as regional standards. Monitoring regional audit trends, addressing past deficiencies, and keeping evidence of discovery closure readily available is key to ensuring consistent alignment across these various regimes.
Indian Ocean MoU kuruldu – Hint Okyanusu: Indian Ocean MoU established – PSC cooperation between Indian Ocean coastal states begins
Indian Ocean MoU, Hint Okyanusu ve çevre: The Indian Ocean MoU coordinates port state control of 18 member states in and around the Indian Ocean; Members spread over a wide geography, from Australia to India, from South Africa to Iran and the coast of East Africa. This region hosts the busiest trade routes between Suez and the Straits of Malacca and a critical portion of the world's oil/container traffic. The MoU shares inspection data through the IOMIS regional system and identifies priority ships through risk-based targeting.
Indian Ocean MoU'nun belirgin bir özelli: A salient feature of the Indian Ocean MoU is the differences in inspection capacity between member states; Therefore, the MoU emphasizes strengthening regional standardization through auditor training programs and technical assistance. Inspection rates may vary depending on the capacity of the member state. Ships entering the region must consider the MoU's common rules as well as strong national regimes: Australia's AMSA and South Africa's SAMSA are known for their own stringent enforcement. As CIC campaigns are coordinated with the Paris and Tokyo MoUs, ships should review current themes and submit gap closure evidence in a timely manner.
Indian Ocean MoU'nun en zorlu yönetişim: The most challenging governance challenge of the Indian Ocean MoU is the extraordinary diversity of its membership base: on the one hand, there are countries with developed flag/port state infrastructure and experienced staff of inspectors, such as Australia, and on the other hand, small coastal states with limited administrative and financial resources, such as Eritrea, Comoros, Sudan or the Maldives. This gap poses the risk of inequity in inspection quality: even though they are bound by the same MoU framework, the number of inspectors, training level and equipment of one member port may be very different from another, threatening the consistency of targeting and deficiency detection. To offset this risk, the MoU attaches structural importance to capacity-building programmes: auditor trainers from experienced member states are sent, common audit manuals and checklists are standardized, IMO technical cooperation funds are directed to auditor training of junior members and infrastructure investment. The aim is that the inspection reflects the same basic quality and consistency no matter which port of call; Otherwise, ship operators may consciously choose weaker regulated ports, weakening the credibility of the entire regime.
Indian Ocean MoU'yu ayıran en belirgin ö: The most distinctive feature that distinguishes the Indian Ocean MoU is the differences in surveillance capacity between member states: the region covers a wide spectrum, from countries with developed PSC infrastructure (Australia, South Africa, India) to countries with limited resources. Therefore, the MoU pays special attention to auditor training programmes, technical assistance and standardization work; The aim is to ensure consistent inspection quality across all member ports. Inspection data is shared through IOMIS (Indian Ocean MoU Information System) and risk-based targeting is based on this data. The region has high control volume and strategic importance as it hosts the busiest trade routes between Suez and the Strait of Malacca; joint CIC campaigns are coordinated with the Paris and Tokyo MoUs.

IOMIS veri paylaşımının pratikteki değer: The practical value of IOMIS data sharing is the ability to uninterruptedly track a ship's footprint within the region. For example, if a ship is inspected at a port in India and flagged as high risk due to a serious structural deficiency, this information immediately reaches other member states via IOMIS; When the same ship calls at an Oman or South African port on its next voyage, the inspector of that port will see the current risk status of the ship and the previous finding, prioritize the inspection accordingly and usually subject it to a more comprehensive inspection. This chain mechanism makes substandard ships visible across the region that a single port cannot catch with its limited capacity, and prevents ship operators from being able to disguise poor performance in one port in another. Because risk-based targeting relies on this shared data, the timeliness and data quality of IOMIS determines the effectiveness of the entire system; Therefore, the MoU considers member states' timely and accurate entry of audit results into the system as an integral part of capacity building efforts.

IOPP Certificate'ın ayrılmaz ve aslında: An integral and indeed the most informative part of the IOPP Certificate is its supplement: Form A for non-tank ships, Form B for tankers. This annex lists all the oil pollution prevention equipment on board: capacity and type of oil-water separator (OWS), 15 ppm monitoring and alarm device, slop tank layout, cargo oil residue monitoring device (ODME), separated ballast tanks (SBT) and crude oil washing (COW) systems. During the inspection, the actual equipment on the ship is expected to match this list exactly; The supplement must be updated whenever a piece of equipment is changed or removed, otherwise there will be a discrepancy between the certificate and the actual situation, which is a PSC finding. Supplement is thus the official inventory of the ship's environmental equipment and the road map for inspection.
IOPP rejiminde en ciddi ihlaller donanım: The most serious violations in the IOPP regime revolve around registry fraud and bypass, not hardware. The devices known as 'magic pipes', which pump the bilge directly into the sea by bypassing the oil-water separator, and their concealment in the Oil Record Book are among the most severely punished maritime crimes worldwide; It results in millions of dollars in fines and imprisonment, especially under the APPS in the United States. It is therefore vital that the ORB is kept accurate, complete and honest. Without IOPP, the ship cannot sail, while MARPOL Annex I non-compliance will result in detention at PSC.
IOPP rejiminin denetlenebilirliğinin kal: The heart of the auditability of the IOPP regime is the Oil Record Book (ORB): Part I records engine room operations (bilge sorting, sludge transfer/burning, bunkering), Part II records cargo/ballast operations on tankers. Each entry indicates the type, quantity, time and location of the operation and is signed by the officer in charge and the master; The ledger is kept on the ship for a certain period of time (usually three years). ORB is one of the first documents examined in the audit because it reveals where and how the discharges are made. The most egregious violations do not revolve around hardware failure but registration fraud and bypass: 'magic pipe' assemblies bypassing the oil-water separator and their concealment in the ORB resulting in millions of dollars in fines and imprisonment under APPS, particularly in the US; Whistleblower rewards encourage the discovery of these violations. Therefore, keeping the ORB honest and complete is the most critical aspect of IOPP compliance.

In the engine room, the oil-water separator (OWS) reduces the oil in the bilge water below the legal limit of 15 ppm, and the 15 ppm alarm automatically stops the discharge when this limit is exceeded. ODM, slop tanks and separated ballast tanks (SBT) monitor cargo discharge in tankers and prevent dirty water from being discharged into the sea. All these operations are recorded in the Oil Record Book (ORB); This ledger is the evidence of pollution prevention and the focus of inspection. SOPEP is a ship-specific emergency response plan against a possible leak.

Regulations such as SOLAS, MARPOL and IGS Code tell what to do; ISGOTT explains step by step how to do this safely in the field. The stakes on tankers are uniquely high: the cargo is flammable, toxic and environmentally harmful, much of the operation is the joint responsibility of ship and shore (or another ship), and a single mistake can be catastrophic. ISGOTT standardizes this shared responsibility; Co-publishing OCIMF, ICS and IAPH ensures that both ship and terminal sides speak the same language. That's why ISGOTT practices are sought as actual reference in vetting audits.
ISGOTT'un kalbi, gemi ile terminal arası: The heart of ISGOTT is the management of the critical interface between ship and terminal. Before starting a transfer, the parties hold a pre-transfer (pre-cargo) meeting: the initial and maximum flow rate (pumping rate), the low flow rate during topping-up, the communication method to be used (VHF channel and backup), the emergency stop (ESD) signal, the maximum allowable manifold pressure and the procedure to be applied if communication is interrupted are clarified. All safety conditions are confirmed by the Ship-Shore Safety Checklist (SSSCL), which is filled out and signed by the ship and terminal representative together. ISGOTT 6 has redesigned this list from a 'box-filling' formality to a process in which each item is actually verified and reconfirmed at regular intervals.

The ISM Code (International Safety Management Code) is the systematic framework for safe ship operation and the master is the sole ultimate implementer of this framework on the ship. SMS (Safety Management System) procedures, risk assessments, near-miss reports, internal audit findings and corrective actions are all under the supervision of the Master. Within the scope of the ISPS Code, it is the Master's responsibility to implement the ship security plan (SSP), manage security level (MARSEC) changes and coordinate with the SSO/CSO/PFSO. This chapter covers the day-to-day implementation of ISM and ISPS systems on board; It deals with concrete procedures, from DOC/SMC certification to major non-conformity management, from MARSEC level transitions to SSAS activation.

Purpose, scope and definitions of the ISM Code.
ISM Code'un amacı: denizde emniyeti sağl: The purpose of the ISM Code is to ensure safety at sea, prevent human injury and loss of life, and protect the environment.
ISM Code'un ilk maddeleri, sistemin zemi: The first articles of the ISM Code lay the groundwork for the system. Article 1 clearly defines the purpose of the code: to ensure safety at sea, to prevent loss of life and injury and to avoid damage to the environment (especially the marine environment); For this reason, it requires every company to set safety targets. Clause 2 requires the company to establish a written safety and environmental protection policy and implement it at all levels of the organization. Article 3 defines the concept of 'company' and highlights a critical fact: ISM covers not only the ship but also the shore organization that operates it. If the owner and operator of the ship are different, the party actually managing the ship assumes ISM obligations and notifies the flag state. Thus, safety responsibility is not left unclear, but is attached to a concrete legal entity.
ISM dış denetiminin en temel mesleki tek: The most basic professional technique of ISM external auditing is to constantly test that the existence of a procedure is not the same as its implementation. The auditor is not satisfied with reading an SMS manual and seeing 'fire drills are held once a month'; It requires concrete evidence to verify this claim: signed drill reports, photographs taken during the drill, whether the crew remembers which task they undertook in that drill, whether the dates of the test records of critical equipment (fire pump, emergency generator) match with the maintenance book. A 'major non-conformity' is not a single forgotten signature; It is a repeated or systemic failure that indicates a break in the system as a whole—situations exceed this threshold, for example, when no internal audit has been performed for months, a critical procedure is unknown to the entire crew, or a DPA is found to be not actually performing its duty. Such a finding could trigger suspension of the SMC (and therefore the DOC) because the auditor's conclusion is no longer 'there is a minor deficiency' but rather 'this system cannot be relied upon to actually work'.

ISPS Code, emniyet (safety – kazalardan: ISPS Code is the first major regulation that clearly brings the distinction between safety (protection from accidents) and security (protection from intentional attacks) into maritime legislation. It was rapidly developed following the September 11, 2001 attacks out of concern that commercial ships and ports could be a tool or target of terrorism. It operates based on SOLAS Chapter XI-2 and adopts a risk-based approach: first, threats and vulnerabilities are assessed (SSA), then concrete measures against them are linked to a plan (SSP). The code treats the ship not as an isolated unit but as a security system together with port facilities.

ISPS uyumu bir değerlendirmeyle başlar:: ISPS compliance begins with an assessment: Ship Security Assessment (SSA) systematically analyzes the threats to which the ship may be exposed and its vulnerabilities to them. This work is carried out under the responsibility of the CSO (Company Security Officer); It identifies critical equipment and areas (bridge, engine room, cargo control, access points), evaluates possible threat scenarios (unauthorized entry, stowaway, sabotage, weapons/explosive smuggling, use of the ship as a weapon) and reveals gaps in existing measures. SSA forms the basis of the ship's security plan; A poorly made evaluation leaves the entire plan based on it unfounded. Therefore, SSA is a disciplined process that combines a concrete site inspection and risk analysis.
ISPS, güvenliği atanmış sorumluluklar ve: ISPS embodies security through assigned responsibilities and daily practices. Onboard SSO is responsible for plan implementation, shoreside CSO is responsible for company level coordination, portside PFSO is responsible for facility security; This trio ensures uninterrupted security at the ship-port interface. In day-to-day operation, access control is central: the identity of everyone boarding is verified, visitors and contractors are registered, the gangway is constantly monitored. Restricted areas (bridge, engine room, radio room, cargo control) are closed to unauthorized access and marked. Security equipment – hidden alarm system (SSAS), AIS, CCTV, lighting and access control equipment – is tested regularly. SSAS is particularly critical: it silently notifies shore authorities in the event of an attack, without alerting the ship.
ISPS, güvenliği belirli kişilere atanmış: ISPS embodies security with responsibilities assigned to specific individuals. On board the Ship Security Officer (SSO) is responsible for the implementation of the security plan; On shore, the Company Security Officer (CSO) provides company-level coordination; On the port side, the Port Facility Security Officer (PFSO) manages facility security. This trio ensures uninterrupted security at the ship-port interface. When responsibilities between the ship and the port need to be clarified, a Declaration of Security (DoS) is signed. The security history of the ship is monitored with Continuous Synopsis Record (CSR).
ISPS: gemi güvenlik planının uygulanması: ISPS: the Ship Security Officer (SSO) is responsible for the implementation of the ship security plan; There is CSO on the shore and PFSO in the port.

Several tools complement the operation of ISPS. A Declaration of Security (DoS) is an agreement signed between a ship and a port facility (or another ship) when security responsibilities need to be clarified – for example, if one of the parties is at a higher security level. Continuous Synopsis Record (CSR) ensures identity continuity by tracking the ship's flag, name, owner and class history and is kept on the ship along with the ISSC. Regular drills (typically every three months) and more comprehensive drills (drills – annually) are carried out to ensure that the plan does not remain on paper. ITC 69, geminin 'büyüklüğünü' parayla ve: ITC 69 translates the 'size' of the ship into a single international language associated with money and safety. There are two basic measures: Gross Tonnage (GT) represents the entire enclosed volume of the ship and forms the basis for regulatory thresholds such as safety requirements, crew numbers, certification types, etc. Net Tonnage (NT) represents only revenue-generating (cargo/passenger) volume and is used in the calculation of commercial cargo such as port fees and canal tolls. The important thing is that these values are volume-based and dimensionless coefficients; It is calculated with the same formula all over the world, unlike inconsistent national systems in the past.
ITC 69, tonajı ölçen idareye göre değişe: ITC 69 transforms tonnage from an estimate that varies depending on the measuring administration into a verifiable mathematical result. Gross tonnage (GT) is calculated by applying a logarithmic coefficient to the ship's total enclosed volume (V, cubic metres): GT = K₁ × V, where K₁ = 0.2 + 0.02 × log₁₀V. The logarithmic coefficient ensures that the contribution of volume to tonnage decreases proportionally in large ships. Net tonnage (NT) represents only revenue-generating (freight/passenger) volume and is calculated with a more complex formula: it includes the parameters cargo volume, draft/depth ratio squared and number of passengers; NT cannot go below certain lower limits. The important thing is that these values are volume-based and dimensionless; Unlike inconsistent national systems in the past (the old Moorsom method), it is calculated with the same formula all over the world and documented with the International Tonnage Certificate.

ITC 69'un pratik önemi, kendi başına bir: The practical importance of ITC 69 lies in the fact that, although it does not establish a safety or environmental rule of its own, it provides the common unit of measurement that determines the scope of almost every IMO convention. A ship learns which articles of these contracts it will be subject to by first looking at the GT value calculated according to ITC 69. For example, the obligation to carry AIS starts at the 300 GT threshold; Many parts of SOLAS for cargo ships (Safety Construction, Safety Equipment certificates) use the 500 GT threshold and MLC 2006 adopts the same 500 GT limit for the Maritime Labor Certificate requirement; The IAPP certification and SOPEP requirement of MARPOL Annex VI is based on a 400 GT threshold, and the EEXI/CII regime increases this threshold to 5000 GT. These thresholds are not arbitrary: they are based on the recognition that the risk posed by large ships, relative to the administrative and technical burden of smaller ships, justifies more severe regulation. Therefore, whether a shipowner keeps GT just below or above a threshold when making a ship design or modification decision is a strategic decision that directly determines which certification and equipment regime it will fall into.

İkinci Mühendis (Second Engineer / 2nd E: As the operational head of the engine room, the Second Engineer is primarily responsible for the daily operation of the main engine, monitoring its performance and early detection of anomalies. This responsibility; It includes daily logging, evaluation of temperature/pressure/rpm/fuel parameters, indicator diagram and PMI (Pressure Measurement Indicator) measurements, cylinder drain oil and scrape-down analysis, scavenge inspection organization and reporting performance monitoring records to the Chief Engineer. This section explains step by step the methodology that the Second Engineer should follow in main engine performance management.
İkinci Mühendis (Second Engineer), makin: The Second Engineer is the day-to-day operational manager of the engine room. He implements the Chief Engineer's directives in the field, manages watch engineers, and is the actual executor of PMS work orders. Daily operation of the main engine, fuel/oil transfers, engine room housekeeping and personnel management are the primary areas of responsibility of this officer. As the most senior officer of the mechanical department after the Chief Engineer, he assumes command of the department in his absence.

Second Engineer is the person who, as the operational head of the engine room, implements the planned maintenance program (PMS - Planned Maintenance System) approved by the Chief Engineer in the field. This responsibility; It includes distributing work orders to watch engineers and machine crews, performing the work correctly/on time/safely, spare parts and consumables management, risk assessment and operation of the permit-to-work system, recording the completed works back to the PMS software and keeping a record chain ready for class/PSC inspection. This section explains step by step the methodology that the Second Engineer should follow in maintenance management.
İkinci Mühendis, gemideki yakıt (FO/DO/V: The Second Engineer is responsible for the safe planning and execution of fuel (FO/DO/VLSFO/MGO) and oil (LO) operations on the ship. This task; It covers SOPEP-compliant preparation of the bunker (refueling) operation, scupper closure and drip tray placement, sampling and density/temperature recordings, internal FO/DO transfers, purifier (separator) operation, settling/service tank management and top-up planning with lubricating oil (LO) consumption monitoring. A single bunker operation carried out incorrectly can result in both serious marine pollution penalties and main engine damage due to faulty fuel. This section explains the operation step by step.
İkinci Mühendis, makine dairesi personel: As the operational supervisor of the engine room personnel, the Second Engineer is responsible for establishing the watch order, standardizing watch handover-handover procedures and workforce distribution. This task; It includes preparation of watch bill, management of UMS (non-watch) and traditional watch patterns, keeping overtime and working/rest hours in accordance with MLC 2006 and STCW rules, fatigue management and maintaining discipline/team morale. A properly established watch pattern is a guarantee of both safety and personnel rights. This section explains this management step by step.
İkinci Mühendis, makine dairesinin opera: As the operational head of the engine room, the Second Engineer is primarily responsible for maintaining cleanliness, order and safety standards on a daily basis. Housekeeping; It is not just an aesthetic issue, it is a safety barrier that directly reduces the risks of fire, slip/fall and pollution. Controlling oil leaks, monitoring oil level, keeping lighting working and escape routes clear; These are items directly evaluated in PSC, vetting (SIRE/CDI) and ISM audits. This section explains step by step how the Second Engineer constructed the engine room layout as a management system.

As the operational head of the engine room, the Second Engineer is directly responsible for the maintenance of auxiliary systems—boiler, purifier, and air compressor. Boiler water treatment and safety valve testing, purifier overhaul planning and air compressor valve/cooler maintenance; This ensures the safe and efficient operation of equipment. A boiler safety valve failure or purifier neglect creates both safety and operational risks. This section covers auxiliary system maintenance.
İkinci Mühendis, Üçüncü/Dördüncü Mühendi: Task distribution, watch order, competency evaluation and training planning of Second Engineer, Third/Fourth Engineer, ETO and machine crews. Coordination of familyization, safety training and vendor-specific training.

İkinci Zabit (Second Officer / Navigatio: The Second Officer (Navigation Officer) is the main responsible for keeping the paper and electronic charts and all nautical publications on the ship up to date, corrected and ready for the voyage. It keeps the chart portfolio constantly updated with Weekly Notices to Mariners (NtM), T&P (Temporary & Preliminary) notifications, NAVAREA/NAVTEX navigational warnings and ENC (Electronic Navigational Chart) update CD/online services. This section; It explains step by step the weekly NtM application, tracing technique, block correction, chart correction log, ECDIS database update, AIO (Admiralty Information Overlay), folio management, CATZOC/source data reliability and record keeping for PSC inspection within the framework of SOLAS V/27 and V/19. Aim; is to set out with a "corrected and approved" chart/publication set each time.

The Second Officer (Navigation Officer) is the officer primarily in charge of passage planning / voyage planning on the ship. With berth-to-berth logic, he prepares the plan consisting of four stages — appraisal, planning, execution and monitoring — submits it for the master's approval and monitors the bridge team's implementation. This section explains step by step elements such as route selection, waypoint determination, UKC (Under Keel Clearance) calculation, no-go area identification, contingency anchorage and abort point determination, parallel indexing and squat within the framework of IMO Resolution A.893(21).

The Second Officer (Navigation Officer) is responsible for keeping regular maintenance, testing and calibration records of bridge navigation devices. Gyro compass error and magnetic compass deviation monitoring, speed log calibration, echo sounder checks, RACON/SART tests with radar performance monitor and verification of proper functioning of ECDIS/AIS/VDR form the basis of this task. This section; It explains step by step the navigational equipment requirements of SOLAS Chapter V, IMO performance standards and daily/weekly/voyage control routines. The aim is to ensure that position and maneuver decisions are based on reliable device data and that a complete record is presented in the PSC inspection.

Second Officer (Navigation Officer) is the natural owner of practical training that improves the navigational competence of the bridge team as well as navigation planning. Bridge Resource Management (BRM) / Bridge Team Management (BTM) drills increase the competence of new officers and trainees (cadets) with ship-specific ECDIS familiarization, radar/ARPA training and COLREG scenarios. This section; Within the framework of STCW Manila amendments and IMO type-specific ECDIS training obligation, it explains error chain, challenge & response, closed-loop communication, situational awareness and automation complacency with concrete drill scenarios. The aim is to transform paper proficiency into real bridge performance.
İkinci Zabit gözetiminde harita düzeltme: Supports chart corrections, passage plan preparation and NAVTEX/NtM tracking under the supervision of the Second Officer. Chart reading, waypoint calculation and UKC control are learned practically.
İkinci Zabit, açık denizde habersizce GP: The Second Officer turns off (or simulates) the GPS input without notice in the open sea. Expectation: the officer of the watch recognizes the alarm, switches to dead reckoning, independently verifies the position with a radar/visual fix, informs the master, and safely keeps ECDIS running in DR mode. In the debrief, response time and accuracy are evaluated.
İkinci Zabit, doğu-batı doğrultusunda ya: The Second Officer is responsible for systematically moving the ship's clock forward or backward during east-west voyages and ensuring that this change is consistently reflected in all official records. Clock change; It has a direct impact on the deck logbook, GMDSS radio recording, rest hour charts and ETA calculations and, if mismanaged, can lead to MLC 2006 rest hour violations or loss of recording continuity. This section; It explains step by step the logic of standard time zones and zone description, when and in which watch the time will be changed, keeping the UTC reference constant, retard/advance concepts and international date line transition within the framework of STCW A-VIII/1 and MLC 2006. The Second Officer prepares a clock change plan with the Master's approval, announces it to the crew and ensures that the rest hours are not violated.
İkinci Zabit, pek çok gemide GMDSS (Glob: The Second Officer serves as the daily responsible for GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) equipment on many ships. This responsibility; This includes performing regular testing of VHF DSC, MF/HF DSC, Inmarsat (FleetBroadband/Fleet One), NAVTEX, EPIRB, SART and portable VHF devices, maintaining a complete GMDSS Radio Log, conducting battery and antenna checks and monitoring spare parts/power supply status. This section; Starting from GMDSS maritime zones (A1-A4), it explains daily/weekly/monthly test procedures, DSC test call logic, distress alert hierarchy and common deficiencies in PSC inspection within the framework of SOLAS Chapter IV.
İkinci Zabit, sefer süresince meteoroloj: The Second Officer is largely responsible for the continuous monitoring and evaluation of the meteorological situation throughout the duration of the voyage. Analysis of NAVTEX, weather fax (radiofax), Inmarsat EGC/SafetyNET weather messages and synoptic charts; Early warning against severe weather conditions, route alternative recommendation and support to the implementation of the heavy weather preparation plan are at the center of this mission. This section; It provides a practical framework from reading pressure systems to weather routing principles, from tropical storm avoidance to ship-specific speed/route decisions. The final route decision always rests with the Master; The Second Officer collects data, analyzes it and prepares a reasoned recommendation.
İkinci Zabit, seyir planlaması ve köprüü: The Second Officer is primarily responsible for navigational planning and bridge operations. Charts, nautical publications, navigational instruments and GMDSS equipment are in the charge of this officer. He works as the bridge's "navigational intelligence": he prepares passage plans, makes meteorological evaluations, follows up ECDIS and radar maintenance, and keeps an active bridge watch in the watch rotation. In accordance with the STCW Code, holding a GMDSS operator certificate is mandatory.
İkinci Zabit, uluslararası pratikte gemi: The Second Officer serves as the ship's medical officer in international drill. In accordance with SOLAS Chapter III and MLC 2006 Rule 4.1, it is mandatory to have adequate medical equipment and medicines on board. Keeping the medical chest inventory up to date, checking the expiration dates of medicines and supplies, keeping the medical log book and preparing supply lists at the port are within the scope of this duty. In case of crew illness or injury, communication with TMAS (Telemedical Assistance Service), patient evaluation and medevac coordination when necessary are carried out by the Second Officer. Organizes medical emergency drills and first aid drills.
İkinci Zabit'in (Second Officer) klasik: The classic watch periods of the Second Officer are 04-08 and 16-20; Since these hours include the transitions between dawn and dusk, they are one of the most critical watches in terms of navigation. The officer of the watch (OOW), as the master's representative, is independently responsible for the safe navigation of the ship within the framework of the collision avoidance regulations (COLREG 1972) and STCW Code A-VIII/2. This section; It explains step by step the principles of lookout, safe speed, collision risk assessment, radar/ARPA plotting, AIS monitoring, position cross-checking, Master call criteria and Bridge Resource Management (BRM) with the requirements of COLREG Rule 5-19 and STCW. It also addresses the specific risks of the dawn/dusk watch, beacon/shape recognition and sound cues, based on professional practice.

İnert gaz iki yoldan üretilir: ya kazan: Inert gas is produced in two ways: either from the flue gas (flue gas, low oxygen) of a boiler or independent burner, or from a nitrogen generator. The flue gas is first washed in a scrubber to remove sulfur and soot particles, and then it is pressed into the tanks with blowers (fans). The system has a critical safety layer that prevents backflow: deck water seal and non-return mechanisms prevent flammable gas in the tank from returning to the engine room; P/V breaker protects the tank from excessive pressure and vacuum. Oxygen analyzers and pressure sensors constantly monitor the system and alarm when limits are exceeded.
İnert gaz ile doldurulmuş tank, oksijens: A tank filled with inert gas is an oxygen-free and potentially toxic confined space. NEVER enter without atmospheric testing, gas freeing and entry permit; Even sticking your head in is fatal.
İnert gaz sistemi farklı amaçlarla, sıkı: The inert gas system is operated in a strict sequence for different purposes: inerting (reducing the oxygen in the tank), purging (diluting flammable vapor by purging it with inert gas), gas-freeing (making the tank safe for human entry by ventilating it), and topping-up (maintaining positive pressure during discharge/navigation). There are critical safety devices that make the system safe: the deck water seal prevents flammable gas from escaping back into the engine room with a liquid barrier, the non-return valve provides an additional backflow barrier, the P/V breaker (pressure/vacuum breaker) protects the tank from excessive pressure and vacuum. Oxygen analyzers and pressure sensors constantly monitor and alarm when limits are exceeded. Inert gas is produced either from boiler/flue gas (washed in a scrubber) or from an independent nitrogen generator; Cargo operation is strictly prohibited when the system is not working and this is a serious finding in both PSC and vetting inspection.
İnert gaz sisteminin en kritik anı, boşa: The most critical moment of the inert gas system is a failure during discharge: when the pumps are evacuating the tank, if the emptied volume is not replaced by inert gas, an in-tank vacuum will occur and there is a risk of structural collapse (tank implosion); Therefore, in case of IG blower or scrubber failure, it is mandatory to stop the discharge immediately and provide controlled air entry into the tank (only with an approved bypass / vent arrangement). The deck seal is a quiet but vital component of the system; If the water level drops, flammable steam can bypass the deck seal and leak into the fan room, so the water level and heating (to prevent freezing) are checked regularly. In a crude oil washing (COW) operation, the tank is kept in an inert gas atmosphere while simultaneously being washed with high-pressure jets; This dual operation makes oxygen monitoring even more critical because static electricity generated during washing and gases dissolved from sludge layers pose additional risks. This is where crew discipline comes into play: oxygen records are kept every watch, operation is immediately stopped at alarm thresholds, and the cargo operation is never 'temporarily' disabled.
İnert gaz sisteminin tüm amacı, tank atm: The whole purpose of the inert gas system is to keep the tank atmosphere in the zone where combustion is impossible. A hydrocarbon-air mixture can only ignite in the flammable range (between the lower explosion limit LEL and the upper limit UEL); However, when the oxygen content is reduced below a certain threshold, ignition cannot occur regardless of the fuel ratio in the mixture. The inert gas goes below this 'critical dilution line', keeping the tank safe: as a general rule, oxygen is kept below 5% in the pumped inert gas, and below 8% in the tank atmosphere before loading/unloading. The tank is always kept at slightly positive pressure so that no air (and therefore oxygen) leaks in from the outside. This logic explains why continuous oxygen measurement and pressure monitoring are at the heart of the operation.
İnert gaz yalnızca bir donanım değil, bi: Inert gas is not just a piece of equipment, but a set of procedures: purging (purging the tank with inert gas), inerting (reducing oxygen) and gas-freeing (ventilating the tank for human entry) are applied in strict order, for different purposes. During loading/discharge the tank is maintained at positive pressure and low oxygen at all times. The crew regularly measures and records the oxygen level, maintains the scrubber/blower, and checks the deck seal water level. It is strictly forbidden to carry out cargo operations when the inert gas system is not working and this is a reason for commercial rejection in PSC detention and vetting (SIRE) inspections.

İstif faktörü (Stowage Factor, SF), bir: Stowage Factor (SF) refers to the volume (m³/t or ft³/t) occupied by a ton of cargo when stowage and is the basic size of load planning. How much cargo a hold can hold and whether the ship will reach its volume or deadweight limit first is directly determined by SF. In the actual stowage, unusable spaces (broken stowage) remain between the loads and due to the ship structure; therefore the net portable amount is always below the theoretical calculation.

İstif faktörü, yükün birim ağırlığının k: The stacking factor is the volume occupied by the unit weight of the load: SF = V / W. Loads with low SF (e.g. iron ore ~0.4 m³/t) are heavy and dense; The ship reaches its deadweight limit before the volume is full (deadweight cargo). High SF loads (e.g. cotton ~2.0 m³/t, timber) are light and bulky; The cargo hold fills up before the ship reaches the weight limit (measurement/volume cargo). The volume required for the load is found by the formula V = W × SF. In planning, it is determined which limit (weight or volume) will be reached first; this drives cargo hold occupancy strategy and revenue optimization.

Kaldırma kuvveti tek başına geminin stab: Buoyancy alone does not determine whether the ship is stable or not; but it is an indispensable prerequisite for stability. If the buoyant force is less than the weight of the ship, the ship sinks; if it is greater, the ship rises. In equilibrium, these two forces are in the same direction and of equal magnitude. However, the positional relationship of the directions—that is, the relative position of the center of gravity and the center of lift—determines the balance character of the ship.

Kaldırma kuvveti, bir geminin su üzerind: Buoyancy is the fundamental physical effect that enables a ship to stay afloat and is directly based on one of the most fundamental principles of fluid mechanics. When a ship enters water, it displaces water equal to its own volume. The weight of this displaced water creates an upward force acting on the ship. As long as this force balances the weight of the ship, the ship maintains its buoyancy.
Kaldırma kuvveti, deniz suyunun yoğunluğ: Buoyancy varies depending on the density of sea water. A ship floating in fresh water sinks more under the same weight; because the density of fresh water is lower than sea water. For this reason, the density of water is always taken into calculation in ship stability and draft calculations. Port changes, river mouths and channel crossings are of operational importance in this respect.

Physically, the center of buoyancy is the center of gravity of the submerged volume of the ship. This point depends on the geometric distribution of the displaced water volume and is completely independent of the ship's center of gravity.

Kapsam yüzdesi geminin seyrettiği güzerg: The percentage of coverage varies depending on the route the ship is on, and it is useful to make this concrete. A voyage from Rotterdam to Hamburg (between two EU ports) is considered intra-EU and all (100%) emissions from the fuel consumed on that voyage are included in the EUA obligation. A voyage from Rotterdam to New York (from an EU port to a non-EU port) is considered extra-EU and only half (50%) of its emissions are covered; The return voyage from New York to Rotterdam is also covered at 50%, the result does not change if the return voyage starts from a non-EU port. In contrast, emissions resulting from the fuel consumed by the ship while it is anchored or berthed (at berth) in the port of Rotterdam are covered 100%, regardless of the voyage route. A voyage from a non-EU port to another non-EU port is completely excluded (0%) because the voyage does not call at an EU port at any point.

Kaptanın iletişim ağı; armatör/şirket (D: Master's communication network; It is a multi-layered structure consisting of the shipowner/company (via DPA), charterer (charterer), port agencies, port authorities, class, P&I, terminal and official authorities. At the center of this network are uninterrupted communication with the Designated Person Ashore (DPA) stipulated by the ISM Code and the "overriding authority" recognized by SOLAS V/34-1 and ISM 5.2. The essential professional balance of the Master is to manage the tension between the commercial demands of the charterer and the safety of the ship/crew; In this process, it is knowing when to say "yes" and when to say "no" and documenting every decision. This chapter discusses the Master's communication discipline with concrete procedures in the context of its legal framework, reporting lines, time/voyage charter distinction, agency coordination and crisis communication.

Kaptanın seyir emniyetine ilişkin soruml: The Master's responsibility for the safety of navigation is one of the oldest and clearest principles of maritime legislation. This chapter introduces the concept of “ultimate liability” not just as an abstract legal principle; It concretely addresses passage planning, bridge discipline, critical decision points, relationship with the pilot, weather routing decisions, abort point management and the practical use of the "overriding authority" right.

Karadeniz limanlarına girecek gemiler, I: Ships entering Black Sea ports should be prepared for initial and detailed inspections based on the IMO PSC Guidelines; Targeting is done according to ship age, type, flag performance and past results. An important point specific to the region is the Turkish Straits: the passage of the Istanbul and Dardanelles Straits in entry and exit to the Black Sea requires compliance with VTS notification requirements and traffic patterns. As the Black Sea MoU conducts CIC campaigns in coordination with Paris and other MoUs, ships should review current campaign themes with the crew and share evidence of closure with the flag state and classification society.
Karadeniz, sınırlı bir su değişimine sah: The Black Sea is more sensitive to pollution than other offshore regions due to being a semi-enclosed sea with limited water exchange; It has limited connections to the Mediterranean and the Sea of Azov, except through narrow passages such as the Bosphorus and Kerch Straits, which slows the rate at which pollutants are removed from the water. The region also hosts heavy dry bulk (especially grain) and tanker traffic; Grain exports from Ukraine and Russia, as well as regional crude oil and product transportation, constantly fill the Black Sea ports. Within the MARPOL framework, there are specific regulations and regional environmental agreements (such as the Bucharest Convention) addressing the environmental sensitivity of the Black Sea; This environmental vulnerability also shapes the control priorities of the Black Sea MoU. Oil log accuracy, ballast water management, waste management plans and operational pollution prevention equipment carry weight in district inspections above the standard PSC scope. For bulk carriers, structural integrity and loading/stowing plans stand out as a special inspection issue because grain cargo carries the risk of slipping into inappropriate stowing.
Karadeniz'e giriş ve çıkış, dünyanın en: Entry and exit to the Black Sea passes through the Turkish Straits (Istanbul and Dardanelles straits), one of the most difficult navigational passages in the world; this is a corridor with heavy traffic, sharp turns and strong currents. Transition requires compliance with the notification and reporting requirements and traffic patterns of the Turkish Straits Vessel Traffic Services (VTS); This is a region where COLREG and navigational safety applications are tested in practice. In terms of PSC, ships must review applicable CIC themes with the crew before entering Black Sea ports, share evidence of finding closure with the flag state and classification society, and take into account their own records in the BS-INFO system where inspection data is shared. The geopolitical dynamics of the region may affect navigation and port access at times; This creates an additional variable in route planning.

Katodik koruma, gövde çeliğinin kendisin: Cathodic protection is based on the principle of sacrificing a metal (zinc or aluminum anode) that is more easily dissolved than the hull steel itself and directing corrosion to these anodes; Melting of anodes over time is the normal and expected operating mode of the system. But the rate and pattern of anode consumption is not a mere regeneration schedule but also a diagnostic tool. The melting of all anodes on the hull properly and close to the predicted rate indicates that the protection system is working properly. However, melting of anodes in certain areas much faster than expected usually indicates one of two problems: either the coating in that area has deteriorated and the steel has been exposed directly to water, causing the anode to send disproportionate current to that point; Or, there is a stray current on the ship caused by a leaky electrical circuit, and this current consumes the anodes faster than normal. When the surveyor notices this pattern, he not only replaces the anodes but also inspects the coating condition in that area or recommends starting a leakage current survey in the electrical system; Otherwise, they will encounter the same abnormal consumption in the next pool period, or even local corrosion on the underlying steel.

Kısıtlı görüş (restricted visibility), d: Restricted visibility is one of the navigation conditions that causes the most loss of life and property in maritime history. COLREG Rule 19 comes into play when fog, heavy rainfall, snow, sandstorms or other similar conditions restrict visibility. The main difference of Rule 19 from all other rules is that it applies to ships approaching without visual contact and eliminates the give-way / stand-on distinction — each ship must maneuver without having a full view of the opposing ship's position and intentions. While this makes radar reading, ARPA analysis and audio signals critical, it also creates a navigational environment where misinterpretations develop more quickly. For maritime students, all the requirements of Rule 19 — speed, radar, sound signals and maneuvering restrictions — must be understood in their entirety.
Kısıtlı görüş alanında veya yakınında, g: In or near the restricted visibility area, regardless of day or night, the following signs are given at a maximum of 2 minutes apart. Bell/gong is used for ships at anchor and aground.

Kısıtlı görüş koşullarına giren gemi içi: Standard procedures for a ship entering restricted visibility conditions: (1) put engines on standby; (2) start sound signals — motor ship: long blast every 2 minutes (Rule 35(a)); (3) place additional spotters on the bridge and redistribute the workload; (4) light all navigation lights; (5) use radar and ARPA at the highest resolution; (6) Activate AIS and listen to channel 16. Within the scope of GMDSS, NAVTEX fog warnings and announcements on the local port channel should be monitored in the waters in question. SMS (Safety Management System) under ISM requires the ship to document fog procedures in writing; The Master must record in the log book that he followed these procedures.
Kısıtlı görüş koşullarında radar ve ses: In conditions of limited visibility, radar and sound signatures are the two primary means of avoiding collision. While radar provides target detection and tracking, sound signals provide positional awareness and warning functions at close range. The effective use of these two tools directly determines the level of safety in restricted visibility.

Kıyı seyri (Coastal Navigation), geminin:
Coastal navigation is a form of navigation in which the ship navigates within visual distance of the shore or within the scope of radar, and continuous position confirmation can be made. Compared to open sea navigation, it offers more safe reference points and involves more traffic, fewer squares and more danger. This contradictory feature makes coastal navigation techniques both a rich and critical subject.

The essence of coastal navigation techniques lies in the principles of determining a reliable position and ensuring sustainable safety. Instead of adhering to a single method, using visual reference, bearing, transit line, clearing line and electronic systems together creates a reliability hierarchy. When there is an error in one method, the other one steps in and reveals the error; This cross-validation approach should be applied throughout the course.
Kıyı seyri planlamasında mevki güncellem: In coastal navigation planning, the frequency of position updates and the variety of methods should be significantly increased compared to the open sea.
Kıyı seyri sırasında görsel yöntemlerin: The combined use of radar and ECDIS, along with visual methods during coastal navigation, creates an integrated verification approach that covers the weak points of each system. Klas sertifikası ile bayrak devleti stat: Class certificates and flag state statutory certificates (documents within the scope of SOLAS, MARPOL) are often confused, but they are legally separate systems. Class verifies, on the basis of a private law contract, that the ship has been structurally and mechanically designed and maintained in accordance with its technical rules; This is not a state authority, but a commercial relationship between the shipowner and the classification society. Statutory compliance, on the other hand, is a public law obligation arising from interstate agreements (SOLAS, MARPOL, MLC) and the final responsibility lies with the flag state. In practice, these two systems overlap to a large extent, as most flag states delegate statutory certification to the classification society in the capacity of RO, and the same surveyor carries out both class and statutory checks in the same visit. However, the overlap is not complete: even if a ship is in class, a deficiency in purely operational/administrative areas such as ISM, ISPS or MLC does not fall within the scope of class and is recorded as a separate deficiency in the PSC. Conversely, class loss automatically becomes a PSC detention because the validity of statutory certificates is often dependent on class approval. Therefore, saying 'it has a class certificate' does not mean 'there is full statutory compliance'; The two are parallel but legally independent layers of assurance.

The Master's B/L signature legally binds the company; Therefore, a signature cannot be made without verifying the amount and apparent order and condition of the load and without "clausing" the suspicious load. Konşimento (Bill of Lading, B/L) üç teme: The Bill of Lading (B/L) serves three basic functions: (1) Receipt — is evidence that the cargo has been received on board the ship in the quantity and condition specified; (2) Evidence of the contract of carriage—reflects the terms between the carrier and the cargo party; (3) Negotiable instrument / document of title - transfer of the bill of lading means the transfer of ownership of the cargo and the cargo is received by presenting the bill of lading. This triple function places the bill of lading at the center of international trade and letters of credit payments.

There are also 'shipped/on board' (confirming that the cargo has been loaded onto the ship) and 'received for shipment' bills of lading. A 'clean' bill of lading does not contain any visible damage/deficiency in the cargo; Registered (dirty) bill of lading carries a damage notice and creates problems in the letter of credit.

The Convention's annexes complete the technical language: Annex I covers colour, angle and range of navigation lights; Annex III specifications for audio signal devices; Annex IV defines danger signs. In this case, each ship slows down to a safe speed, keeps the machines ready for maneuver and makes systematic observations with radar. When maneuvering against a ship detected solely by radar, two behaviors should be avoided: turning to port to a ship ahead of oneself (other than ahead) and changing course to approach a ship in cabin/sideline or astern of oneself. Appropriate fog signals are also given when visibility is limited. Rule 19 is one of the most critical rules in practice due to the fact that the majority of accidents occur in poor visibility and is directly linked to STCW's radar/ARPA training requirements.

No sudden maneuvers should be made on the basis of the radar signature alone: Rule 19(d)(i) states that 'if a ship determines the risk of collision solely on the basis of the radar signature, she must refrain from taking course to port alone' — because if a ship coming from the bow and shoulders takes course to port the two ships may have turned in the same direction. Kural 2, COLREG'in 'istisnai koşullara k: Rule 2 is COLREG's 'opening the door to exceptional circumstances' clause: it expressly recognizes that no other provision of the contract excludes the consequences of negligence and that it may be necessary to deviate from the rules to avoid unusual danger. This article also envisages the profile of a Master who evaluates and judges the situation in its entirety rather than blindly following the rules. Although COLREG rules give clear instructions for certain situations (crossing, head-on, overtaking), it is not possible to foresee all scenarios in the open sea; Rule 2 closes this loophole. In practice, the concept of 'good maritime practice' is widely used in court decisions: what would a reasonable Master do in these circumstances? Internalizing this standard provides a much more permanent professional competence than memorizing the rules.

Kural 5, geminin görme ve işitme dahil m: Rule 5 requires the ship to keep a constant and effective lookout by all available means, including vision and hearing; ARPA and AIS are among these tools, but relying solely on their technological output is insufficient. 'Continuous' lookout requires all bridge personnel, including the officer of the watch, to remain situationally aware. Rule 6 imposes the obligation to apply 'safe speed' in all circumstances; Safe speed is the maximum speed at which the ship can stay within full stopping distance, taking into account current visibility, traffic density, wind, current and water depth. For ships not fully maneuverable — draft restriction, machinery failure — the safe speed is reduced accordingly. Safe speed becomes particularly important in restricted visibility: Rule 19(b) expressly requires speed commensurate with the radar range.

Leeway (wind drift) is the phenomenon in which the actual path (COG - Course Over Ground) followed by the ship, under the influence of wind force, deviates towards the leeward from the route indicated by the ship's heading. In other words: although the ship steers in a certain direction, the wind pushes it laterally and the actual track deviates from the intended course.

Leeway is expressed in degrees and is always in the leeward direction; That is, in a northerly wind (upwind = north, leeward = south) the ship slides south. The magnitude of the Leeway angle; It depends on wind strength, ship's freeboard height, speed and ship form.

Therefore, leeway calculation is done in practice by a combination of observation and estimation methods.

LLC'nin 1988 Protokolü, sözleşmenin dene: The 1988 Protocol of the LLC introduces the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC), which puts the audit architecture of the convention on the same schedule as SOLAS and MARPOL. Before the protocol, since each contract had its own survey and certificate renewal cycle, a ship might have to receive more than one inspection visit on different dates in the same year. The HSSC and Load Line Certificate also fall into a common five-year certification cycle and annual/periodic surveys can be scheduled to coincide with the windows of SOLAS's Safety Construction and Safety Equipment surveys and MARPOL's IOPP/IAPP surveys (usually ±3 months of the main date). In this way, the classification society can check the ship's watertightness, structural integrity and pollution prevention equipment together in a single survey visit. The protocol also standardized the display of the free board mark and tonnage marks on the certificate and strengthened the certificate recognition between state parties. In practice, this means that survey planning for ship management should not be considered separately LLC but within a single annual program together with the SOLAS and MARPOL survey schedule.

LRIT (Long-Range Identification and Trac: What is the main purpose of the LRIT (Long-Range Identification and Tracking) system?

LRIT (Long-Range Identification and Tracking) is a system established within the scope of SOLAS for remote identification and tracking of ships on a global scale. While AIS is a local/in-range broadcast system, LRIT transmits a ship's identity and location via satellite as a closed (secret) data stream to authorized states. In this respect, LRIT differs from open broadcast AIS in terms of both purpose and privacy.

LRIT cihazı, geminin kimliğini, konumunu: The LRIT device automatically transmits the ship's identity, position (latitude/longitude) and date-time when the position was received. Standard reporting typically occurs several times per day (e.g., every 6 hours); However, data centers can remotely increase the reporting frequency or request location information instantly (on-demand polling) according to the request of the monitoring state. This flexibility allows for more frequent tracking when a ship approaches a certain area or in a special situation. Unlike AIS, LRIT data is not publicly available; only authorized parties can access.

LRIT ile AIS arasındaki temel fark nedir: What is the main difference between LRIT and AIS?
LRIT ile AIS sıkça karıştırılır ancak fa: LRIT and AIS are often confused, but they solve different problems. AIS broadcasts locally and openly over VHF; its range is limited to the radio horizon and its primary purpose is collision avoidance and local situational awareness (anyone can listen). LRIT, on the other hand, provides global coverage via satellite, produces less frequent reports, and its data is confidential/available only to authorized states. In summary, AIS is for 'ships to see each other'; LRIT is for 'states to monitor ships remotely'. The two do not replace each other, they complement each other.

Each flag state uses a National/Regional/Cooperative or International Data Center. The information flow between data centers is routed through the International Data Exchange (IDE) managed by IMO. Which ship data a state can access is regulated according to the Data Distribution Plan (DDP) determined by IMO; Thus, each state only has access to the data of ships flying its own flag, approaching its coast or coming to its port.

Makine Stajyeri (Engine Cadet), denizcil: Engine Cadet is a candidate engineer who is on a ship to complete the marine internship part of maritime training in the mechanical department. By completing the sea service period stipulated by the STCW Code, he/she receives practical training on the way to Watch Engineer qualification. The intern has no authority or signature responsibility on board; however, he/she is expected to participate in all machine operations at an observation and support level. Training Record Book (TRB) is the official document of this process.
Makine stajyeri (Engine Cadet), STCW Böl: The Engine Cadet participates in engine room duty under the direct supervision of the Engineer Officer of the Watch (EOOW) to gain STCW Part A-III/1 competency areas practically on the ship. This participation; Includes parameter reading, log book recording, liquid level control, alarm recognition, engine room round routine and teamwork. The intern has no authority to make independent decisions or keep independent watches; Every intervention, every switching and every unusual situation is made with EOOW approval. This section explains step by step the methodology, regulatory framework and safety limits that the trainee must follow in supervised watch participation.
Makine stajyeri vardiyaya bir karar veri: The mechanical trainee joins the watch not as a decision maker, but as an observer-executor receiving training. A clear understanding of authority limits is the basis of safety.
Makine stajyeri, gemide geçirdiği her se: The mechanical intern must document each sea-service period he spends on the ship with an official Sea Service Certificate signed by the Master. This document is the main evidence in proving the period of sea service required for the OOW (Officer of the Watch — Machinery) qualification certificate of STCW. In addition, obtaining a Watchkeeping Certificate for the Engine Department requires that all competency areas within the scope of STCW Table A-III/1 be completed in TRB and approved by the instructor engineer. Loss or irregularity of documents may mean that the internship period is not recognized or the examination right is postponed. This section explains step by step the structure of the Sea Service document, the sea service calculation, the certification process and document management.

The mechanical trainee must document each sea-service period spent on the ship with an official Sea Service Certificate signed by the Master. Loss of documents may mean that the internship period is not recognized or the right to take the exam is postponed.
Makine stajyeri, gemideki acil sistemler: The mechanical trainee must learn the operation and test procedures of the emergency systems on the ship as an observer. These systems; It covers emergency generator, emergency fire pump, emergency air compressor and emergency steering gear tests. The intern also learns the remote operation principles of quick closing valve, emergency stop and ventilation flaps, and how to follow the blackout recovery procedure step by step. These systems are the last line of defense to maintain the safety of the ship when normal power and control are lost. This section describes each system's function, testing logic, and regulatory requirement.
Makine stajyeri, gemideki sistemleri anl: The mechanical trainee must gain two key skills to understand the shipboard systems and manage maintenance: reading technical drawings and using Planned Maintenance System (PMS) software. Technical drawings; It provides a "map" of the system with documents such as piping diagram, electrical diagram and general arrangement. PMS is the digital core of maintenance work planning, work order opening/closing, spare parts coding and stock control. This chapter explains the drawing reading methodology, symbols, and PMS workflow step by step.
Makine stajyeri, geminin can damarı olan: The mechanical trainee must practically learn the fuel oil and lubricating oil systems, which are the lifeblood of the ship. This learning; It includes supervised monitoring of bunker (fuel supply) operation, FO/DO settling and service tank systems, purifier (separator) operation, LO sump and circulation circuit. The intern also learns fuel/oil sampling, observation of viscosity and density measurement, and the logic of filling by reading the Oil Record Book (ORB) Part I format. These systems are critical for both the reliability of the machine and the prevention of marine pollution within the scope of MARPOL. This section explains step by step the operation of the systems, control points and regulatory requirements.
Makine stajyeri, makine dairesinin yükse: The mechanical trainee must systematically learn basic safety procedures in order to work safely in the high-risk environment of the engine room. These procedures; It includes energy isolation (LOTO - Lockout/Tagout), work permit system (PTW - Permit to Work), enclosed space entry, hot work and personal protective equipment (PPE) use. In addition, the intern; Learns emergency procedures such as blackout rescue, engine room fire and flooding, escape routes and muster station information and actively participates in drills. This chapter explains step by step the rationale for each safety procedure, its regulatory basis and the trainee's role in drill.
Makine stajyeri, pompa overhaul, valf ba: The machine intern participates as an assistant in maintenance work such as pump overhaul, valve maintenance, filter replacement, gasket cutting, heat exchanger cleaning and bolt torqueing. The purpose of this participation is; learning the names and functions of equipment parts, gaining correct tool use and dexterity, becoming familiar with the technical language and experiencing the safe conduct of maintenance work. The intern does not carry out care independently; Works within the scope of work order and permit under the supervision of the responsible engineer or experienced oiler/fitter. This section details the methods, safety steps and learning strategy that the trainee should follow in care support.
Makine stajyeri; ana makine, yardımcı ma: Mechanical trainee; Learns systematically the main engine, auxiliary machinery (generators), boiler, air compressors, separator/purifier, pumps, heat exchangers and pipe/valve systems. This learning; It includes reading the piping diagram, physically determining equipment locations, recognizing the operating principle of each system, safety devices and alarm points. The aim is to understand the engine room not as a collection of parts, but as a whole of interrelated systems. This chapter provides a framework for the trainee to learn machine systems in a layered and logical manner.

Malta ve Kıbrıs gibi AB üyesi Akdeniz de: For Mediterranean EU member states such as Malta and Cyprus, being covered by both the Mediterranean MoU and the Paris MoU/EU PSC Directive may seem, at first glance, to be an unnecessary overlap; But in practice, these two layers do not repeat each other, they reinforce each other. Provides access to Europe's extensive PSC network via the Paris MoU framework, THETIS infrastructure and NIR risk profile; The Mediterranean MoU framework includes the same ship in a separate inspection and data sharing network of non-EU coastal states in North Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. When a ship calls at the port of these two member states, the inspection result is reflected in both systems and becomes visible to inspectors both in Europe and the wider Mediterranean basin. This means spreading the impact of a single audit across two regional networks; A substandard ship would be flagged not only in EU ports but also along the entire Mediterranean coast from Algeria to Lebanon. Therefore, dual membership operates as a mechanism that reduces the burden of supervision but increases coverage and deterrence.

Mammatus, bulut tabanından aşağı sarkan: Mammatus are bag- or sac-shaped protrusions that hang down from the cloud base; It is seen in its most striking form under the cumulonimbus anvil. While normal cloud bases are formed flat by rising air, mammatus are the product of sinking cold, moist air—meaning there are strong downdrafts and severe turbulence in that layer of the atmosphere. Seeing Mammatus often means there is a mature, strong Cb cell nearby; It can be seen both in front of and behind the storm. Message for sailors: the convective system in the region is severe, the risk of sudden gusts and wind shifts is high; Caution must be maintained even if the system appears outdated.

MARPOL kirliliği önlemeyi düzenlerken OP: While MARPOL regulates pollution prevention, OPRC regulates what to do when precautions are not enough. The Exxon Valdez disaster demonstrated the devastating consequences of being caught unprepared for a major spill: without response equipment, planning, and coordination, oil irreparably destroys coastlines and ecosystems. The OPRC therefore requires advance preparation at both ship and national level. The Convention treats pollution as a matter of 'if' rather than 'what if' and pre-defines everyone's role. The 2000 OPRC-HNS Protocol also expanded the scope to hazardous and harmful substances.

Metasentrik nokta, geminin küçük yatma a: The metacentric point is one of the basic geometric reference points used to define the stability behavior of the ship under small heel angles. When the ship is upright, the direction of the buoyant force is represented by a vertical line passing through the center of buoyancy. When the ship tilts at a very small angle, the center of buoyancy shifts to a new position and the direction of buoyancy passing through this new point intersects with the initial direction at a point. This intersection point is called the metacentric point and is usually denoted by the letter M.
Metasentrik nokta, yalnızca küçük yatma: The metacentric point is a concept that is valid only for small angles of repose and is therefore used in “initial stability” or “small angles stability” analyses. As the angle of heel increases, the path followed by the center of lift ceases to be linear and the metacentric approach loses its validity. The metacentric point therefore defines the initial heeling behavior of the ship, not the large angles stability.

Metasentrik yüksekliğin büyüklüğü, gemin: The size of the metacentric height also determines the movement character of the ship. Ships with very large GM values are called “hard” ships; These ships make fast and short-term rolling movements. This may increase structural loads and negatively affect personnel comfort. In contrast, ships with very small GM values are defined as “soft” ships; Periods of roll are long and the ship exhibits slow, reluctant movements. Excessively small GM values bring the risk of loss of stability.

Metasentrik yükseklik ise ağırlık merkez: Metacentric height refers to the vertical distance between the center of gravity and the metacentric point and is denoted by GM. This distance directly determines whether the ship will behave stable or unstable at a small angle of heel. When the metacentric height is positive, the metacentric point is located above the center of gravity and the ship is considered stable. When the metacentric height is zero, the center of gravity and the metacentric point coincide and the ship is in indifferent equilibrium. When the metacentric height is negative, the metacentric point remains below the center of gravity and the ship behaves unstable.

At higher frequencies the 'sky wave' predominates: the wave reaches the ionosphere, refracts back to earth and can reach thousands of miles away. MLC 2006, beş Title etrafında örgütlenir: MLC 2006 is organized around five Titles, each securing a different dimension of the seafarer's life. Title 1 establishes the minimum conditions for work on board: minimum age (16, with stricter limits for night and hazardous work), valid health certificate, vocational training and regulated recruitment/placement services. Title 2 covers the conditions of employment: written Maritime Employment Agreement (SEA), regular wage payment, working/rest hours, leave entitlement and repatriation. Title 3 governs the fact that the ship is a living space: cabin, ventilation, lighting, dining and recreation standards. Title 4 covers health protection, medical care, occupational safety and social security. Title 5 regulates compliance and implementation (certification, audit, complaint mechanisms). Each Title consists of binding Standards (Part A) and guiding Guidelines (Part B).
MLC 2006, denizcilerin onurlu ve adil ko: MLC 2006 provides for seafarers to work in dignified and fair conditions. The D&A process must be conducted in accordance with the principles of confidentiality, registration and fair consideration, even while applying zero tolerance; Otherwise, it creates both legal and reputational risks.

MLC 2006, gıdanın yeterli miktar, besin: MLC 2006 requires food to be provided in sufficient quantity, nutritional value, quality and variety and free of charge. Budget discipline is no excuse for lowering this standard; the cook balances the two together.
MLC 2006, mürettebata yeterli ve güvenli: MLC 2006 requires crews to be provided with adequate and safe drinking water; Water quality should be monitored and hygiene records kept.
MLC 2006, SOLAS, MARPOL ve STCW'nin yanı: MLC 2006 sits alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW as the 'fourth pillar' of maritime law; because while the former regulate the ship and professional qualifications, the MLC directly protects the humane working and living conditions of the seafarer. It combines 68 separate conventions and recommendations within the ILO into a single consolidated text. Its structure is built around five Titles, and each Title consists of binding Standards (Part A) and guiding Guidelines (Part B). The strength of the convention comes from the principle of 'no more favorable treatment', which subjects a ship to both flag state inspection and port state control: even a ship of a flag that has not ratified the MLC is inspected in an MLC member port.

MLC 2006'nın tasarımında bilinçli bir es: There is deliberate flexibility in the design of the MLC 2006: rather than imposing the same rigid pattern on each country's legal system, administrative structure and existing legislation, the convention allows different means of implementation that achieve the same protective goal. This is called 'substantial equivalence' and is embodied in DMLC Part I. For example, a standard may stipulate a certain minimum square footage of seafarer accommodation; Instead of strictly applying this minimum square metre, a country may adopt an alternative regulation (e.g. a different space-to-person ratio, additional common space compensation) adapted to its ship types and climatic conditions, but which equally protects the seafarer's overall quality of life and privacy; This is conditioned on the ILO being informed of the justification for this difference and demonstrating that the alternative provides 'exactly equal' protection of the standard. This flexibility is an important reason why the MLC has been able to bring more than 100 flag states around the world with different legal and shipbuilding traditions into the same contract; A rigid, one-dimensional set of standards would not find such broad acceptance.
MLC Certificate (Maritime Labour Certifi: MLC Certificate (Maritime Labor Certificate) is a certificate that certifies that a ship meets the working and living conditions standards within the scope of MLC 2006. While SOLAS certificates document the ship and STCW document the competence of the crew, the MLC Certificate directly ensures the humane working conditions of the seafarer. Mandatory for international expedition ships of 500 GT and above; It is issued by the flag state or authorized classification society after compliance with the 14 MLC control areas is verified. It is valid for five years and is subject to an interim audit in the middle of the term.

MLC sertifikasyonunda en sık denetlenen: The most frequently inspected and most frequently deficient area in MLC certification is working/rest hours. The rule applies with a limit of either maximum work (maximum 14 hours in 24 hours, maximum 72 hours in 7 days) or minimum rest (minimum 10 hours in 24 hours, minimum 77 hours in 7 days); The rest can be divided into two parts at most and one part should be at least 6 hours. These hours are recorded daily for each sailor and a copy is given to the sailor. It is essential that the records reflect reality: records that appear compliant on paper but actually conceal overwork are violations of both MLC and STCW and have serious consequences in the PSC inspection. These rules closely match the fatigue provisions of the STCW; because fatigue is both a seafarer's right issue and a direct safety risk.
