STCW Code'un teknik kalbi, yeterliliği ö: The technical heart of the STCW Code is the competence tables that make competence measurable. For each task, tables are defined with columns 'competence – knowledge/understanding/skills – demonstration method – assessment criteria'; Thus, 'a good officer of the watch' ceases to be an abstract qualification and is reduced to countable and testable competencies. The contract divides the duties into seven functions (navigation, cargo handling, ship operations/life safety, machinery, electrical, maintenance, radio) and treats each function at three levels of responsibility: operational (watch officer), management (master/chief engineer and chief officers) and support (auxiliary personnel – ratings). A person's certificate shows which level of competence he/she is in which function; This structure establishes a consistent language of competence across the world.

STCW, denizdeki kazaların büyük çoğunluğ: STCW was born from the fact that the vast majority of accidents at sea are human-caused. Before the convention, each country applied its own proficiency standard; A Master's certificate valid in one country could be considered insufficient in another flag. STCW solves this chaos by placing seafarer training, certification and watchkeeping standards on an international minimum basis. Its structure is two-layered: the Convention text, which contains mandatory provisions, and the STCW Code, which gives technical details. The Code is divided into binding Part A and advisory Part B. In this way, 'competence' ceases to be an abstract concept and is reduced to measurable knowledge-skill-attitude tables.

STCW'nin Chapter VIII'i sadece kimin var: Chapter VIII of the STCW regulates not only who can keep a watch, but also under what circumstances. Recognizing that fatigue is a safety risk, minimum rest hours are defined: at least 10 hours of rest in 24 hours and at least 77 hours of rest in 7 days. These hours are recorded and checked frequently during PSC inspections. The principle of 'fitness for duty' includes alcohol/drug limits and duty readiness. Watchkeeping handover procedures, lookout and bridge/engine room watchkeeping are also defined in this section; these rules directly overlap with COLREG's lookout requirement.
STCW'nin gücü, sertifikaların gerçekten: The power of STCW comes from the fact that the certificates are truly trustworthy; Therefore, the contract regulates not only education but also the quality control of education. Competencies are proven through approved simulators (ECDIS, ARPA, engine room), structured on-board training record books and standardized assessments. Certificates are not indefinite: they must be revalidated, typically every five years, with sufficient sea service or an approved refresher course; In particular, tanker endorsement and safety training is refreshed periodically. To protect the integrity of the system, the IMO maintains a 'white list' of countries that effectively comply with the requirements; A seafarer's certificate must also be recognized by the endorsement of the flag that employs him. Use of false certificates is heavily prosecuted and certificate/record non-compliance with port state inspection may result in the detention of the ship.
STCW'nin öngördüğü yetkinlik alanlarını: Fills out the TRB on a daily basis, covering the competency areas prescribed by STCW. Every mission, observation and training module is recorded. SUA hukuki çatıyı kurarken, denizdeki gü: While SUA establishes the legal framework, daily protection at sea is provided by operational guidelines such as BMP (Best Management Practices). In high-risk areas such as the Gulf of Aden, West Africa and Southeast Asia, ships take speed and route measures, install physical barriers such as barbed wire and water cannons, prepare a citadel (safe room) where the crew can take shelter, and immediately warn the coastal and flag state in case of attack. SUA is the legal superstructure that ensures that the attackers will be prosecuted and not go unpunished in case these measures fail and an attack occurs; Together with the ISPS Code, it forms two complementary pillars of maritime security.
SUA Sözleşmesi, 1985'te Achille Lauro yo: The SUA Convention was established in response to the inadequacy of international law against terrorism and illegal acts at sea, following the seizure of the Achille Lauro cruise ship by armed men in 1985 and the killing of a passenger. There was a gap because the classical definition of piracy (for private gain, on the high seas, from one ship to another) did not cover many modern attacks. SUA fills this gap: it criminalizes acts such as violence against the ship, crew or passengers, seizing the ship and endangering the safety of navigation, and obliges states to prosecute these crimes.

SUA'nın 2005 Protokolü, sözleşmeyi 11 Ey: SUA's 2005 Protocol significantly expanded the scope of the convention by adapting it to the post-9/11 threat environment. New crimes include using a ship to carry weapons of mass destruction (nuclear, chemical, biological) or the materials used to make them, using the ship as a weapon (e.g. to crash into a facility), and creating a threat of death/serious injury by emitting hazardous materials from the ship. The most practical innovation of the Protocol is the boarding procedures introduced by Article 8bis: a state may request permission from the flag state to stop and search on the high seas a ship flying the flag of another state and suspected of being involved in an SUA crime; The flag state can determine in advance how and when it will respond to this request. This mechanism opens a legal way to intervene in illegal shipping on the high seas without violating state sovereignty.
SUA'nın temel ilkesi 'ya yargıla ya iade: The basic principle of SUA is the 'try or extradite' (aut dedere aut judicare) rule: party states must either try an SUA criminal found in their territory in their own courts or extradite them to another state that will try them; Thus, these crimes are prevented from going unpunished. Agreement; It defines jurisdiction rules based on flag, country and citizenship affiliation and interstate mutual legal assistance mechanisms. SUA is an important complement to the fight against piracy: the classical definition of piracy in UNCLOS (for private gain, on the high seas, from one ship to another) does not cover many modern attacks (incidents in territorial waters, political attacks, actions within a single ship); SUA fills this gap and criminalizes violence against the ship. Şamandıra sistemi IALA düzenine göre yor: The buoy system is interpreted according to the IALA scheme and the world is divided into two main regions. Zone A; It covers Europe, Africa, most of Asia and Australia — Türkiye is in Zone A and remains on the red port and green starboard at the entrance to the port. Region B; It covers North and South America, Japan, Korea and the Philippines, and the lateral colors are THE OPPOSITE: when entering the port, red stays on starboard and green stays on port (“red right returning” as American sailors memorize it). The critical point here is that this statement is not a color sentence, but a transition instruction. Since the same color can represent different sides in different regions, the first reflex when seeing a buoy symbol on the chart is to instinctively ask "which IALA region am I in?" Even though the region changes, the hull shape does not change: the port marking is cylindrical (can) in both regions, the starboard marking is conical in both regions; When color cannot be read, shape and vertex still give accurate information. Although the chart often plots the buoy as a dot, that dot represents the edge of a corridor, the direction of navigation of a hazard, or confirmation of the line of approach; Therefore, the purpose of the symbol is not to inform, but to move.

Şiddetli tropikal siklonlarda (genellikl: A structural process frequently observed in severe tropical cyclones (usually Category 3 and above) is the eyewall regeneration cycle. Outside the existing eyewall, a second concentric eyewall ring forms with a radius of 50–100 km. The outer ring cuts off the flow of moisture and momentum that feeds the inner eyewall, weakening it and collapsing over time; Then the outer ring narrows and becomes the new eyewall. The cycle typically lasts 12–36 hours, during which the system's peak wind speed temporarily decreases. However, this weakening should never be read as a sign of relief for sailors; The cycle has two critical operational consequences. First, the maximum wind radius increases: even if the system loses some peak intensity, the gust area spreads over a much larger area, meaning the 'danger zone' widens, not narrows. Second, once the cycle is complete, the system often rapidly intensifies again. Blurring of the eye and double ring appearance in satellite images is reflected in the bulletins of forecast centers as the expression 'eyewall replacement'; When the route planning officer sees this statement, he should revise the CPA (closest passing distance) calculation according to the expanding wind area.

TBT yasağının uygulamaya geçtiği 2003-20: During the 2003-2008 period, when the TBT ban was implemented, shipowners practically had two options. The first was to completely scrape off the existing paint containing TBT and repaint it with a TBT-free anti-fouling system during a planned dry-dock period of the ship; This was the most permanent solution, but scraping was costly and time-consuming and required special disposal because the scraping waste itself contained TBT. The second was the sealant application, which was an interim solution recognized in the contract for ships that had not yet reached a dry-dock period suitable for scraping: a sealer coat was applied over the existing TBT paint, which physically prevented the TBT from leaking into the water, thus complying with the ban without changing the paint. The choice between these two options depended on the ship's dry-dock schedule, the condition of the paintwork and the cost calculation. This historical pattern forms a direct template for the same binary option (sealant or teardown) recognized today for cybutryne in the 2023-2026 transition period.
TBT'nin sızma mekanizması ve imposex kan: TBT's leakage mechanism and imposex evidence
TBT'nin zararı, boyanın işlevinin ta ken: The harm of TBT stems from the very function of the paint: its anti-fouling effect is based on the continuous and controlled leaching of the biocide from the hull surface into seawater, so that organisms trying to adhere to the surface cannot do so by being poisoned by constantly low doses. However, this leakage is not limited to the hull perimeter; TBT accumulates by dissolving in water and precipitating into sediment and bioaccumulates in the food chain, meaning that at each level the organism carries a higher concentration of TBT than the previous one. The 'smoking gun' evidence that triggered the ban in scientific circles was the imposex phenomenon observed in sea snails (specifically the Nucella lapillus species): female snails exposed to TBT were disrupted in their hormonal system and began to develop male reproductive organs, leading to female sterilization and the collapse of some populations. This observable, repeatable, and directly attributable effect to TBT concentration has provided regulators with hard data proving that TBT is not just a localized but a persistent and widespread ecosystem threat.

Tehlikeli yarım dairede bulunan gemi, rü: The ship in the dangerous semicircle moves away from the cyclone at the highest possible safe speed, taking the wind to its starboard bow. In the semicircle where Navigation can be made, the wind is taken from the Stern stern quarter and passed behind the cyclone. A ship in the direct path of the cyclone aims to quickly move out of the way. In all these manoeuvres, it is necessary to take into account sea state, cargo securing and machine capacity limitations; At extreme speed, Navigation can cause slamming and structural damage.

The ship in the dangerous semicircle must move away from the cyclone, taking the wind to its starboard bow. Navigation can be made, and in the semicircle, the wind is taken from the Stern stern quarter and an attempt is made to move behind the cyclone. The ship in the direct path of the cyclone should aim to move to the right side of the road (Northern Hemisphere) at the highest possible speed. Tidal stream (gelgit akıntısı), denizler:
Tidal stream is the horizontal water movement caused by the periodic water height change (tide) in the seas. Although the tidal movement is up and down, this movement turns into horizontal currents due to the coastal geometry and basin shape. Tidal flowing water is defined by the parameters set (current direction) and drift (current speed, in knots).

Tidal streams are periodic and change direction, unlike permanent currents such as river currents or ocean circulation. In a tidal cycle, the current changes in both speed and direction: it currents in one direction during the falling tide, while the HW begins to current in the opposite direction with the rising tide after a period of slack water. This periodic character makes the tidal stream predictable; Tidal atlas and current tables provide hourly advance information on currents at each location.

Slack water is the best time for maneuvering in narrow channels and straits; because the current force is minimum and the side force on the ship has decreased.

Tidal window (gelgit penceresi), bir gem:
Tidal window is the time period during which sufficient water depth is available for a ship to safely enter or exit a port or canal with a certain draft value. Especially in shallow bars, channel entrances and ports where the tide is decisive, the tidal window forms the center of the entire operational calendar.

Tidal window calculation is a natural continuation of the UKC calculation: the tidal height that satisfies the minimum UKC condition is found and it is determined when this height is exceeded, for how long it is exceeded, and when it falls below it again. This period is the tidal window; The entry/exit operation must be completed within this window.
Tidal window (gelgit penceresi), bir lim: Tidal window is the time period during which the minimum water depth required to enter or exit a port is achieved. The calculation includes the following steps: (1) Minimum required water depth = Draft + Squat + Air allowance + Minimum UKC. (2) Tidal height providing this depth = Minimum required water depth − Chart depth. (3) Using the tidal table and the rule of 12s or the tidal curve, it is calculated when this tidal height is reached and how long it remains above that level.
Tidal window bazı limanlarda ETA’nın en: Tidal window constitutes the strictest restriction of ETA in some ports.
Tidal window belirlendikten sonra liman: Once the tidal window is determined, sufficient time should be left for the port agent, pilot, tugboat and on deck to prepare for the port operation. A realistic tidal window plan includes the following allowances: (1) Early entry allowance: instead of entering immediately after the window opens, waiting an additional 30–60 minutes increases the UKC margin. (2) Operating allowance: unexpected speed losses during transit, traffic delay or pilot coordination time must be taken into account. (3) Margin of safety: tide forecast does not include meteorological influence; Storm surge or low pressure can lower the expected water level by 0.5–1.0 metres. Therefore, meteorology-based water level prediction should also be used during critical transitions.

Title 1 ve 2, istihdam ilişkisinin temel: Titles 1 and 2 govern the basis of the employment relationship. Every seafarer must have a written Maritime Employment Agreement (SEA) clearly stating the terms of duty and pay; The fee must be paid regularly (usually monthly) and a detailed calculation document must be given to the seafarer. The minimum age is 16 and stricter limits apply to night work and hazardous work. Working/rest hours are governed by a limit of either maximum work (14 hours in 24 hours, 72 hours per week) or minimum rest (10 hours in 24 hours). These limits comply with the fatigue provisions of STCW and are controlled by the same records.
Title 2, kaptanın günlük olarak en çok t: Title 2 is the area the Master touches most on a daily basis: contract, wages, work-rest and repatriation.
Title 3 ve 4, geminin bir işyeri olduğu: Titles 3 and 4 govern the fact that the ship is a living space as well as a workplace. Cabin dimensions, ventilation, lighting, food quality and recreation facilities are subject to minimum standards. Health protection; It covers onboard medical care, medicine cabinets, shore medical advice when necessary and evacuation arrangements in serious cases. One of the strongest provisions of the MLC is the right of repatriation: the seafarer must be repatriated free of charge at the end of the contract or in cases of abandonment. With the 2014 amendments, this right was supported by mandatory financial assurance that comes into effect in case of bankruptcy of the shipowner.
Title 5, sözleşmenin kâğıt üstünde kalma: Title 5 establishes the control architecture that ensures that the contract does not remain on paper. International expedition ships of 500 GT and above must carry the DMLC (Part I indicates state requirements, Part II indicates company measures), which includes the Maritime Labor Certificate issued by the flag state and the company's declaration of compliance. Seafarers should have access to retaliation-proof grievance procedures that operate both on board and ashore. Under port state control, MLC violations (unpaid wages, overwork, poor accommodation) are recorded as deficiencies and, in serious cases, the ship may be detained. Thus, MLC transforms seafarer rights from an abstract declaration into an auditable compliance system.

Tokyo MoU de 2014'ten itibaren Paris ben: Tokyo MoU also implements a Paris-like New Inspection Regime (NIR) from 2014: ship risk profile (SRP) is calculated from flag and class performance, ship age/type, operator performance and past inspection results, and the inspection interval is determined accordingly. The most rational approach for a ship entering the region is to check its risk profile through APCIS in advance, review the current CIC campaign themes with the crew, and analyze past deficiencies and eliminate recurring ones. Detention criteria and deficiency codes are aligned with the Paris MoU, thus maintaining a consistent auditing standard between the two regions.
Tokyo MoU ile Paris MoU aynı temel mantı: Although the Tokyo MoU and the Paris MoU share the same basic logic — the HRS/SRS/LRS risk classification and associated inspection intervals — the numbers do not exactly match. In the Paris MoU, a low-risk ship (LRS) falls within a priority window of 24-36 months, while in the Tokyo MoU, this range is 18-30 months; meaning that even a ship deemed low risk in the Asia-Pacific may be targeted slightly more frequently than in Europe. Although the ranges are broadly similar in the HRS and SRS bands, some weightings that go into the risk profile (e.g. regional flag performance lists) may highlight different groups of ships in the two regions; A flag may be on the White list in Paris but in a different order in Tokyo. This difference has a practical consequence for an operator sailing between two regions: the same ship may face a different inspection frequency depending on which region it sails in, even if it has the same actual risk level. Therefore, fleet managers should monitor each region individually according to its own thresholds, rather than a single general risk profile; Achieving LRS status in one territory does not automatically guarantee the same treatment in another. Although data sharing between the two MoUs helps reduce this difference, it does not eliminate it completely.

Tokyo MoU, Asya-Pasifik bölgesindeki 21: The Tokyo MoU coordinates port state control of 21 member states in the Asia-Pacific region and covers waters through which some of the world's busiest container and dry cargo traffic passes. It is the largest PSC region in the world in terms of annual inspection volume; It carries out tens of thousands of inspections every year. It shares the same basic philosophy as the Paris MoU: sharing inspection results through a common database (APCIS), sharing the inspection burden among members, and monitoring substandard ships across the region. The two MoUs work closely together and frequently run joint CIC campaigns.
Tokyo MoU, denetim hacmi bakımından düny: The Tokyo MoU is the world's largest PSC area in terms of inspection volume and covers waters through which the vast majority of world ship traffic passes; This scale creates both an intensive control capacity and a statistically rich database. Another feature of the region is the economic and administrative diversity among member states: countries with developed inspection infrastructure (Japan, Australia, Singapore, South Korea) coexist with countries that are developing capacity. Therefore, the Tokyo MoU places emphasis on auditor training and technical coordination, as well as common standards. The most rational approach for ships entering the region is to check their risk profile in advance through APCIS, prepare for current CIC contact and correct past deficiencies; Thanks to alignment with the Paris MoU, this preparation applies to both regions.
Tokyo MoU'nun bilgi sistemi APCIS (Asia-: The Tokyo MoU's information system, APCIS (Asia-Pacific Computerized Information System), corresponds to the Paris MoU's THETIS: it shares inspection results, ship risk profiles and detention records among member states. The two MoUs not only operate in parallel, they are deliberately harmonized: risk profile calculation parameters, deficiency codes and detention criteria are largely common, and joint CIC (Intensified Inspection Campaigns) are conducted. This harmonization is important because many ships sail in both regions; Thanks to consistent standards, performance in one region is relevant in the other and ships can comply with both regimes with a single preparation. Data sharing ensures that a substandard ship caught in one region can be tracked in another.

Since the Suez and Panama canals implement their own commercial tonnage systems (SCNT and PC/UMS) separate from ITC 69, ships passing through these canals also carry separate canal tonnage certificates and tolls are calculated based on these special tonnages. Tonnage Certificate (International Tonna: Tonnage Certificate (International Tonnage Certificate) is the document that formalizes the gross tonnage (GT) and net tonnage (NT) of the ship within the scope of ITC 69. GT represents the total closed volume of the ship, NT represents the revenue-generating cargo/passenger volume; Both are volume-based, dimensionless measurements. This certificate is a silent but pervasive reference in maritime: port duties, pilotage fees, taxation and many international regulations depend on these values. It is mandatory for international expedition ships of 24 meters and above.
Tonnage Certificate, diğer sertifikalard: The Tonnage Certificate, unlike other certificates, is not timed: it remains valid indefinitely unless there is a structural change, because the result does not change unless what it measures (the volume of the ship) changes. However, when a permanent modification is made that changes the closed volume of the ship (addition/removal of superstructure, cargo hold conversion), it is mandatory to re-measure the tonnage and issue a new certificate; Otherwise, the certificate does not reflect the truth and becomes invalid. Some countries may deny port entry to ships missing tonnage certificates. During the inspection, the declared GT/NT values are expected to be consistent with the certificate and other documents of the ship (manning, safety thresholds).
Tonnage Certificate'ın süresiz geçerlili: The indefinite validity of the Tonnage Certificate means that, unlike other certificates, it does not run the risk of expiry; because the quantity it measures (the closed volume of the ship) does not inherently change over time, whereas a piece of safety equipment becomes obsolete or a management system needs to be updated. However, this permanence is not unconditional: structural interventions that actually change the enclosed volume of the ship invalidate the certificate and re-measurement becomes mandatory. Typical examples of this include the complete closure of a deck (e.g. building a permanent superstructure over an open working deck), the addition of a new deck floor, the conversion of a previously open space (e.g. a container below-deck space) to a permanently enclosed volume, or a major conversion that changes the primary use of the ship (conversion of a dry cargo ship to a tanker or container ship). When one of these changes is made, the shipowner must engage a class or authorized tonnage measurement expert to have the new volume officially measured and obtain a new certificate; Otherwise, the declared GT/NT will remain an incorrect figure that does not reflect the true condition of the ship, and if this situation is detected during the inspection, it will constitute a serious deficiency.

The ESD system is always ready, stopping the transfer within seconds in case of emergency. Even a single drop of oil spilling into the sea activates SOPEP and the terminal/port authority is immediately notified. Bunkering is also subject to the same principles and is carried out with a bunker safety checklist. Mooring is a separate physical hazard: the breaking of a taut line is fatal to personnel standing in the 'snap-back' area; ISGOTT regulates the identification, marking and safe line management of these areas. Thus, ISGOTT gathers the entire operational chain from the tanker's berthing to its departure within a single security framework.

Trilaterasyon, bir noktanın konumunu, ko:
Trilateration is a method of determining the location of a point using distances to multiple reference points whose location is known. The main difference from triangulation is that triangulation is based on angle measurement, while trilateration is based on distance measurement. GPS applies the principle of trilateration on a global scale; The positions of the satellites are known exactly and the distances to the receiver are measured by signal delay time.

The basic geometric logic of trilateration can be explained as follows: if you are at a distance r₁ from a single point of known location, you can be anywhere on a sphere (or circle in 2D) of radius r₁ centered on that point. When a second reference point is added, the intersection of two spheres creates a circle. Adding the third reference results in two points. Earth conditions make either of these two points meaningless; thus, a single location is determined.
Trilaterasyon, mesafe ölçümünden konum b: Trilateration is a method of determining location from distance measurement; triangulation uses angle.
Trilaterasyonun doğruluğu yalnızca mesaf: The accuracy of trilateration depends not only on distance measurement precision but also on the geometric distribution of reference points (satellites). If the satellites are well distributed in the sky, each measurement provides constraints from different directions and the location is determined precisely. If satellites are clustered together, the reflection of measurement errors to the location becomes larger.

This calmness has led many sailors throughout history to make fatal mistakes: the eye is temporary, and then the second half of the storm comes from the opposite direction and in full force. This topic; It examines in detail the physics of the eye, the structure of the eyewall surrounding it, the eyewall renewal cycle, and the decisions a ship encountering the eye must make on the bridge.

The Saffir-Simpson scale (Categories 1–5) classifies hurricane intensity according to wind speed. In Category 5, winds exceed 137 knots.

Turn radius (dönüş yarıçapı), bir gemini:
Turn radius is the radius of the circular arc that a ship follows when it makes a full turn at a given rudder angle and speed. Rudder angle, ship speed and hydrodynamic characteristics of the ship determine the turning radius. A small turning radius indicates high maneuverability.

The concept of turning radius is the basic input of route planning in narrow channels, straits and in-harbor maneuvers. How many meters in front of a waypoint a heading change begins depends directly on the turning radius. Ship righting delay (advance) and transverse slip (transfer) amounts are also part of the turning characteristic.

UKC (Under Keel Clearance – Omurga Altı:
UKC (Under Keel Clearance) is the height of the water column between the ship's keel and the seabed. If this value reaches zero, the ship runs aground; Therefore, UKC is one of the most basic critical indicators of navigational safety. The actual UKC at any given moment is a combination of multiple factors, including chart depth, tide height, ship draft, squat and swell allowance.

UKC calculation is especially critical at port entrances, narrow channels and shallow waters. Most companies set a minimum UKC policy under the ISM Code; This policy is usually expressed as fixed values such as 10–15% of the draft offshore and 0.5–1.0 meters in ports. Going below these limits is considered unsafe.

Ultrasonik kalınlık ölçümü (UTM), bir çe: Ultrasonic thickness measurement (UTM) is based on the principle that a probe placed on a steel plate calculates the thickness by measuring the return time of sound waves from the opposite surface; This is a practical method that quantifies corrosion loss without cutting or damaging the steel. The measurements are not random, but concentrated around the 'critical structural areas' (CSA) that carry the ship's structural load the most and are most exposed to corrosion: areas such as double bottom structures, ballast tank interior surfaces, hold bottom corners and deck beams. Close-up survey, on the other hand, goes beyond measurement: the surveyor physically approaches these structural elements with a scaffolding or rafting (staging/rafting) and looks for defects that cannot be detected by measurement, such as cracks, deformations or welding defects, visually and, if necessary, with non-destructive testing (NDT). As the ship ages, this focus becomes tighter: regions that were sparsely sampled in youth are systematically scanned in middle and older age, because fatigue and corrosion is a nonlinear process that accelerates over time, and past measurement trends are the only reliable way to predict the future rate of deterioration.

Usta Gemici (AB — Able Seaman) ve Gemici: Able Seaman (AB) and Ordinary Seaman (OS) make up the deck department's workforce. Their primary duties are bridge lookout and steering watch during navigation, cargo securing operations in the port, deck maintenance work and support to cargo operations. AB title requires certain period of sea service and proficiency examination under STCW; OS is the more inexperienced crew category.
Usta Gemici (AB), can güvenliği zincirin: Able Seaman (AB) is the field enforcer of the life safety chain; He/she is present at the muster station, performs the duties assigned in the drills (lifeboat team, fire party, boundary cooling, first aid transportation, etc.), uses LSA equipment such as life jacket/immersion suit and EEBD correctly, knows the escape routes and supports the maintenance of his/her own safety equipment. In accordance with SOLAS Chapter III and the LSA/FSS Code, these tasks are reinforced with regular drills; Survival in a real emergency depends on the reflexes and discipline gained in drill. This section; It explains step by step the muster and task card system, major drill types, use of LSA equipment, fire response roles, escape and communications, and equipment maintenance responsibility from an AB perspective.
Usta Gemici (AB), gemiye güvenli erişimi: Able Seaman (AB) is the field implementer of the installation, use and assembly of equipment such as gangway, accommodation ladder and pilot ladder that provide safe access to the ship. Safety net, lifebuoy (with heaving line), adequate lighting and preparation of the pilot boarding arrangement in accordance with SOLAS requirements are directly related to life safety; Every year, falling and drowning accidents occur due to pilot ladders and gangways. This section; It explains step by step gangway and accommodation ladder installation, pilot ladder and combination arrangement requirements (SOLAS V/23, IMO Res. A.1045(27)), preparation of safety equipment (net, lifebuoy, light), pilot transfer operation and typical accident lessons from an AB perspective.
Usta Gemici (AB), güverte alanlarının te: The Able Seaman (AB) is responsible for keeping deck areas clean, tidy and safe; This task is not cosmetic, but a direct matter of life safety and seaworthiness. Clear and unobstructed escape routes, accessible safety equipment, working drainage channels, scuppers and freeing ports; It makes the difference in surviving an accident. A messy deck causes slip/trip/fall accidents, a clogged scupper causes water accumulation on the deck and risks stability, and a closed escape route causes death in fire. This section; It explains step by step the principle of deck layout and "good housekeeping", escape route and equipment access, drainage/scupper/freeing port management, slip-trip risk control and regular cleaning program from an AB perspective.
Usta Gemici (AB), kapalı mekan girişi (e: Able Seaman (AB) generally undertakes standby duties outside during enclosed space entry operations; This task can be even more critical than the intruder because it is the key to rescue and alarm. AB; He maintains a lifeline, maintains constant communication, knows how to use the atmosphere measuring device, and immediately raises an alarm at any sign of discomfort/exit of the person inside. If rescue is necessary, they act by donning an SCBA and calling in additional personnel before entering — because unplanned "hero rescue" attempts have created a second (and third) victim in the majority of enclosed space fatalities rather than saving the first. This section; It explains step by step confined space hazards, enter permit and atmosphere testing, standby duty, communication and lifeline discipline, proper rescue protocol, and "rescuer becomes victim" cases.
Usta Gemici (AB), yük operasyonlarında g: The Able Seaman (AB) is the implementing force of the deck crew in cargo operations; It supports hatch cover opening/closing, cargo lashing/securing, hatch cleaning and preparation, tank soundings and draft readings. These works are directly related to life safety, ship stability and the safe arrival of the cargo to the port; Incorrect lashing or incorrect draft reading can cause serious accidents and commercial damage. This section; It explains step by step the safe conduct of hatch cover operations, lashing equipment and CSS Code principles, hatch preparation and cleaning standards, draft survey and sounding support, on-deck cargo safety and typical accident lessons from an AB perspective.
Usta Gemici (AB); direk (mast), baca (fu: Able Seaman (AB); It works in high and/or sea-facing areas such as masts, funnels, cargo cranes, hatch coaming and oversides. These jobs carry the risks of falling and man overboard, which are among the leading fatal accidents in maritime. Study; It is carried out in accordance with Permit to Work, the twin lanyard seat belt is fastened correctly, the fall arrest system is used, the life buoy + life rope is kept in standby during overside work and the suitability of weather/sea conditions is mandatory. This section; It explains step by step the risk assessment of working at height/overside, the Permit to Work system, fall arrest and harness discipline, scaffolding/chair/bosun's chair and overside equipment, MOB preparation and typical accident lessons from an AB perspective.
Usta Gemici (Able Seaman / AB), köprüüst: The Able Seaman (AB) is the "eyes and hands" of the bridge navigational watch; As a lookout, he undertakes environmental lookout, and as a helmsman, he undertakes the accurate and timely execution of course commands. In accordance with COLREG Rule 5, every ship must maintain appropriate visual and audio look-out at all times, both day and night, in all visibility conditions; The field implementer of this task is the AB. This section; It explains step by step the lookout reporting discipline, standard helm orders, compass/route tracking, night vision and blind spot management, watch reinforcement according to weather/visibility conditions, and watch handover procedure.
Usta Gemici (Able Seaman / AB), yanaşma,: The Able Seaman (AB) is the primary operator in the field of the bow or stern station in docking, unberthing and anchoring operations; He personally carries out line/wire usage, winch operation, heaving line throwing, bollard/bitt mooring and tug mooring and untying operations. These operations involve some of the most frequent and deadliest seamanship accidents; Especially snap-back zone (the area where the line is thrown when it breaks), winch grabbing and crushing injuries continue to claim lives every year. This section; It explains step by step the logic of the mooring scheme, line/wire behavior, winch and bollard techniques, heaving line and tug operation, command discipline and safe work area management from a field perspective.

Üçüncü Zabit (Safety Officer) için drill: For the Third Officer (Safety Officer), the drill is living proof of the ship's emergency preparedness. It cannot be drilled and "passed"; A good Safety Officer manages the drill in three stages: before (is the equipment ready, is the personnel distribution/station bill clear, is the scenario realistic), during (was the correct procedure followed, is the timing kept, are the deficiencies noted) and after (what error occurred, what will be corrected, what will enter the log). During the PSC inspection, sometimes the record is not looked at at all; "Where is your muster station?" and "How do you start the rescue boat engine?" is asked. It's not the equipment that's booming here, it's the training. This chapter covers the SOLAS Chapter III muster and drill regime, scenario design, recording discipline, and the pitfalls of "looking done".
Üçüncü Zabit (Safety Officer) için muste: For the Third Officer (Safety Officer), the muster list is the constitution of the emergency organization: it determines, name by name, who will do which task, in which emergency situation, at which station. This task does not end with hanging the paper; It involves ensuring that each crew member knows their station and mission by heart, knows the relevant equipment (portable VHF, EPIRB/SART, first-aid party equipment, boundary cooling hoses) and reaches the right place within seconds in a real abandon ship, fire or man-overboard scenario. A muster list hanging on the board but not internalized is a dead piece of paper that is useless in the emergency room.
Üçüncü Zabit (Safety Officer) sadece bir: The Third Officer (Safety Officer) is not just a "recording officer"; It plays an active and critical role according to the station bill in emergency situations such as fire, man overboard (MOB) or abandoned ship. Typical duties include forward fire team leadership, boundary cooling coordination, rescue boat preparation, lifeboat boarding control, head count and distress equipment transfer. This section discusses the Safety Officer's emergency response role.
Üçüncü Zabit (Safety Officer), ISM Code: In accordance with the logic of the ISM Code, the Third Officer (Safety Officer) is responsible for ensuring that each new member of the ship quickly adapts to safe operation and that this is recorded. Safety familiarization; It covers where the new crew can get their life jackets, the muster station, fire alarm buttons, escape routes, emergency escapes, fire/watertight door usage and the reporting chain, being shown and documented with a signature. STCW requires basic safety familiarization before or immediately after joining the ship; These records are tangible and auditable evidence of safe operation.
Üçüncü Zabit (Third Officer / Safety Off: Third Officer (Safety Officer) is the officer directly responsible for ensuring that the life-saving appliances (LSA) on the ship are complete, intact, accessible and recorded. This task goes much deeper than simply saying "the equipment has been looked at": it involves verifying that abandon ship equipment such as lifeboats, liferafts, life jackets, life buoys, pyrotechnics, immersion suits, EPIRBs and SARTs are in place, sealed, not expired, freely accessible, the service certificate is valid and the physical condition is consistent with records. The most common defect is that the equipment is in place but its registration is missing; When the PSC catches this, it treats it as "not maintained".
Üçüncü Zabit / Safety Officer, geminin y: The Third Officer / Safety Officer is responsible for ensuring that the ship's fire-fighting equipment (FFE) is intact, functional and usable. This package; It includes portable fire extinguishers, hoses, nozzles, hydrants, SCBA, EEBD, fireman's outfit, fixed CO2/foam/water mist systems, fire alarm system, fire detection and fire control plan. The value of fire equipment consists of three pillars: “being there” (presence), “being functional” (function), and “being able to use it” (competence). The last leg can only be achieved through regular drilling and familiarization.
Üçüncü Zabit / Safety Officer, SOLAS III: The Third Officer / Safety Officer is responsible for planning, executing and recording the weekly and monthly safety tests prescribed by SOLAS III/20 and onboard maintenance guides (MSC.402(96), manufacturer's instructions). This routine; It includes weekly lifeboat inspection and engine run, general alarm test, emergency lighting control, selected fire station tests, monthly extinguisher/SCBA/EEBD checks and expiry list update. A disciplined testing schedule keeps the equipment ready at all times and provides an uninterrupted chain of audit records.
Üçüncü Zabit, birçok gemide Safety Offic: The Third Officer is appointed as the Safety Officer on many ships and is the de facto responsible for the LSA (Life-Saving Appliances) and FFE (Fire-Fighting Equipment) systems. His responsibility is not to "know the equipment"; o ensuring that the equipment is in working order at all times, that records are kept properly, that personnel can use it and that this can be proven against the survey/PSC. Lifesaving appliances and fire-fighting equipment are mandatory on board under SOLAS Chapters III and II-2; Their technical requirements are determined by the LSA Code and FSS Code. ISM Code aims to systematize their maintenance, registration and safe operation.
Üçüncü/Dördüncü Mühendis (Third/Fourth E: The Third/Fourth Engineer is the person directly responsible for the daily and periodic maintenance of the auxiliary machinery in the engine room. This scope; It includes pumps (ballast, bilge, transfer, service), compressors (starting air, service air), separators/purifiers (FO, LO, sludge), boiler (auxiliary boiler) and simple electrical/mechanical maintenance works. This section explains step by step the methodology of performing routine tasks such as valve overhaul, gasket replacement, bearing control and filter cleaning correctly, planned (PMS) and safely.
Üçüncü/Dördüncü Mühendis, ballast tank o: Third/Fourth Engineer takes an active role in the execution of ballast tank operations, bilge level control, OWS (Oily Water Separator) operation and tank soundings on the engine room side. Üçüncü/Dördüncü Mühendis, makine dairesi: The Third/Fourth Engineer is responsible for the periodic testing of engine room safety devices: bilge high-level alarm, oil mist detector (OMD), bearing temperature alarm, over-speed trip, LO low-pressure alarm/trip and FO heater high-temperature alarm are the main ones. These devices are an automatic protection layer that prevents catastrophic failures (crankcase explosion, bearing jamming, overspeed) of the main engine and auxiliary machinery. This section describes the operating principle, test method, acceptance criteria and recording discipline of each safety device.

The Third/Fourth Engineer is the eyes and hands of the engine room watch on the field. Monitors the operating parameters of the main engine, generator (auxiliary engine), boiler, air compressors and service pumps at regular intervals; It records temperature, pressure, level, speed and alarm conditions. Detects abnormal trends early, reports immediately to the Second Engineer or Chief Engineer on duty, and fully implements the watch handover procedure. This section explains step by step the machine watch standard and daily parameter monitoring methodology under STCW.

Vetting denetiminin çıktısı, üye şirketl: The output of the vetting audit is a report shared with member companies; In other words, all potential charterers can see the negative observations in a single inspection. Observations that are not closed prevent the ship from taking on new business, poor performance increases insurance premiums, and terminals may not accept the ship. The decrease in the company's TMSA score spreads the problem from a single ship to the entire fleet. That's why ships conduct a rigorous internal audit (pre-vetting), keep documentation flawless, and especially prepare key personnel (Master, chief engineer) for questions in CAQ format. Vetting is a commercial gateway as decisive as regulatory compliance in modern tanker operations.
Vetting ve iç denetimlerde, düzenli ve s: In vetting and internal audits, night instructions kept regularly and concretely; It is viewed positively as evidence of a strong watchkeeping and ERM culture.
Vetting, devletlerin değil ticari aktörl: Vetting is a layer of control carried out not by states but by commercial actors (oil companies, charterers, terminals). Its logic is simple: the party that will entrust its cargo to a ship wants to see for itself that that ship complies with the standards; because the responsibility and reputational damage of a tanker accident also reflects on the cargo owner. So vetting is actually mandatory, although not mandatory: a tanker without a vetting approval cannot find work. SIRE (oil/gas tankers), CDI (chemical tankers) and OVID (offshore ships) are the standardized formats of this inspection; Unlike PSC and class, it evaluates the ship at the threshold of 'commercial excellence' rather than 'minimum compliance'.
Vetting determines the commercial life of the ship. Master; Must know the new digital structure of SIRE 2.0, RightShip's scoring logic and the place of CDI in chemical transportation.
Vetting'in var olma nedeni, petrol şirke: Vetting's raison d'être is that oil companies have learned the hard way that an accident becomes the responsibility of not only the ship owner, but also the company carrying the cargo, which often has a much higher brand value. Incidents such as Exxon Valdez (1989) showed that even if a tanker's flag and class are compatible, it can be involved in a serious accident, and the clean-up costs, legal liability and reputational damage of this accident will be reflected on the company renting the cargo. After this experience, the oil majors no longer considered it sufficient for a tanker to meet only the 'legal minimum compliance'; According to their own commercial risk appetite, they established an independent audit layer that evaluates elements that the statutory system does not measure (crew practice, maintenance culture, operator history). This is not a regulatory obligation but a purely commercial risk management decision: a company can inspect another company's ship and say 'if it doesn't meet our standards you won't carry our cargo'. SIRE is a standardized, shared version of this logic and so does not replace PSC or class, but adds a commercial filter on top of them.

The Viña del Mar Agreement (Acuerdo Latinoamericano) is Latin America's first regional port state control agreement, coordinating controls in South, Central America and the Caribbean with 14 member states. It was established inspired by the Paris MoU model and shares audit data through the CIALA regional information system. The region has a unique dynamic: Panama, which has the world's largest ship registry, is located in this geography, so there is an intense interaction of both port state and flag state roles in the region.
Viña del Mar Agreement bölgesinin kendin: A unique dynamic of the Viña del Mar Agreement area is that Panama, which has the largest ship registry in the world, is located here. This leads to a heavy intertwining of flag state and port state roles in the region: a significant proportion of ships crossing the region are Panamanian-flagged, so these ships are subject to both their own flag state obligations and the PSC inspection of their port of call. For Panama-flagged ships, it is particularly important to ensure that their flag state inspection and certification processes align with port state expectations. This context ensures that the regional PSC not only inspects foreign flags but is directly related to the quality of a globally widespread flag registry.
Viña del Mar Agreement'in 14 üye devleti: The 14 member states of the Viña del Mar Agreement range widely in terms of supervisory capacity and resource level: from large and relatively developed maritime administrations such as Brazil and Mexico to smaller Caribbean and Central American states with more limited financial and human resources. This difference can lead to disparities in auditor training level, access to audit equipment, and even how consistently risk profile calculations are applied. CIALA attempts to close this gap in two ways: first, it creates a minimum common language by ensuring that all members have access to the same audit data and deficiency codes through the regional information system; Second, auditor trainers and common checklists are provided from more experienced member administrations through IMO's technical cooperation programmes. This effort is not linear and rapid — capacity gaps have not been completely closed — but aims to bring audit quality in the region closer to a more consistent line over time; Thus, which member port a ship calls at should not significantly change the inspection rigor it will encounter.
Viña del Mar bölgesini diğer MoU'lardan: The most striking feature that distinguishes the Viña del Mar region from other MoUs is that Panama, which has the largest ship registry in the world, is both a flag state and a port state geographically located within the operation zone of this MoU. In most large open registries (such as Panama, Marshall Islands, Liberia) the flag state function is geographically separate from the territory in which the ship actually sails; but in the case of Panama this distinction disappears. A Panamanian-flagged ship transiting the Panama Canal and calling at regional ports is simultaneously under two different inspection lenses: the certification and inspection responsibility of its own flag and the PSC inspection of a Viña del Mar member port state—and this port state can often be Panama itself. This dual position gives Panama extra motivation to maintain the quality of its registry, since the detention of a ship in its registry in its own port directly affects the international reputation of the registry. For other member states in the region, this situation creates both familiarity and the need for careful monitoring, brought about by heavy traffic with Panamanian flags.

Although it may seem harmless, it carries an important dynamic warning: the evaporation of precipitation in a layer of dry air rapidly cools that layer, and the heavier air can turn into violent downdrafts (dry microbursts). In other words, virga indicates that there may be sudden and violent, short-term wind bursts on the sea surface below. XTE (Cross Track Error) refers to the vertical (transverse) distance of the ship's current position from the planned route line. If the ship deviates to the right of the course, a positive (+) XTE value is reported, if it deviates to the left, a negative (−) XTE value is reported; Direction sign may vary depending on navigation software. It is automatically calculated and displayed in ECDIS and GPS receivers.

XTE is one of the most basic tracking parameters of passage planning. During the planning phase, the XTE limit is determined for each route segment; This limit refers to the half-width of the safe corridor determined on both sides of the route line. ECDIS generates an alarm when the XTE exceeds this limit.

Yük hattı çizgisinin ihlali, teorik bir: Violating the load line line has much more severe consequences than a theoretical rule violation. If a ship's load line mark is found to be submerged under port state control, this is considered one of the most serious categories of deficiencies in PSC inspection and usually leads to direct detention, with the ship not being allowed to leave the port until it unloads excess cargo or adjusts its ballast. The consequences for insurance and P&I clubs are also severe: policy conditions often require the ship to sail within the legal load line limits; In case of an accident or loss during overloading, the P&I club and Hull&Machinery insurer may refuse to pay compensation on the grounds that the ship is not seaworthy or may recourse to the shipowner through subrogation. Maritime history has painfully shown why freeboarding is so strictly protected: In the 19th century, overloading of British coal ships and sinking of hundreds of them every year started Plimsoll's struggle, and in the modern period, loss of stability due to incorrect stowage and overloading in bulk and dry cargo ships led to serious accidents. That's why load line inspection is a step that should never be missed on the Master's pre-loading checklist.
Yük Hattı Sözleşmesinin tüm mantığı tek: The entire logic of the Load Line Agreement is based on a single concept: freeboard, that is, the minimum height between the deck edge and the water surface. This distance determines the ship's reserve bilge volume and therefore its ability to remain at sea without sinking. The struggle led by Samuel Plimsoll over the sinking of overloaded ships in the 19th century resulted in the 'Plimsoll brand' drawn on the ship's board. LLC turns this idea into an international standard: the maximum allowable loading for each ship is made visible by load line markings on the side and under no circumstances can it be loaded below this line.
Yük hattı, keyfi bir çizgi değil, ayrınt: The load line is not an arbitrary line but the result of a detailed engineering calculation. The calculation begins with a table (tabular) freeboard value according to the type of ship: Type A ships (tankers carrying liquid bulk cargo, small deck clearance) are assessed with lower freeboard, while Type B ships (others) are assessed with higher freeboard. This base value is adjusted by a number of correction factors: correction for the block coefficient (Cb), correction for the ship's depth (D), discount for the closed length of superstructures and forecastles, ship's sheer and bow height. The resulting freeboard represents the ship's reserve bilge volume and therefore its ability to remain at sea without sinking. This calculation is documented on the ship's Load Line Certificate and determines the position of the markings on the side.

High pressure systems are often slow moving or located in semi-permanent positions (Azores High Pressure, Siberian High Pressure, etc.). But high pressure does not always mean calm seas: strong pressure gradients formed at the edges of the system can reach significant wind speeds. Additionally, when high pressure prevails, there is a risk of poor visibility due to radiation fog or inversion layer.

The relationship between these three quantities makes it possible to predict how far the ship will travel along a given route and in what time. When wind and current effects are neglected in plane navigation, ship motion is considered as uniform linear motion at constant speed and calculations are based on this assumption. Therefore, the time-distance-speed relationship is the mathematical core of dead reckoning position determination. In maritime, speed is expressed in knots, and 1 knot equals 1 nautical mile per hour. Distance is in nautical miles, time is in hours.
